subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should take into full account the budgetary reality of the provinces and municipalities involved in Royal Canadian Mounted Police contract negotiations and therefore be prepared to negotiate a contract for RCMP services which does not unfairly transfer policing costs from the federal government to provincial and municipal governments.
He said: Madam Speaker, for the benefit of members and people watching this debate, we in the NDP are calling on the government to renegotiate in good faith fair policing contracts for those provinces which use the RCMP as their provincial and municipal police forces.
We believe this is an extremely urgent issue for Canadians because it touches on some of the most important issues that Canadians are debating today.
First and foremost is the national unity debate. As a result of Tory ideology, which has undermined or destroyed many of the national institutions and symbols that Canadians hold dear, such as the national passenger rail service, Canada Post, the privatization of Air Canada and Petro-Canada and the continuing attack on the CBC, many Canadians feel that the symbols and the structures underlying Canadian unity have been undermined almost to the point of destruction by implementation of Tory policy.
The Tories have justified their attack on Canadian institutions by saying that these institutions cost too much in this day and age. As many political observers have said, Tories seem to know the cost of everything and
the value of nothing. As a result, this country is facing its worst and possibly its last unity crisis.
The second issue in terms of the debate on the RCMP police contracts is the way that the Tories have handled the crisis in budgets and programs of the federal government. The recent Tory budget has cut back on transfers to the provinces, transfers which support cost-shared programs such as hospitals, post-secondary education, social services and other programs in the provinces in order to maintain a decent and level standard of equality services all across this country. As a result of those federal cutbacks, Canadians in various parts of the country are going to be receiving different qualities of service based on the ability of the provinces to support.
The Tories have also cut back income support programs such as family allowance and old age pensions, which are also seen as the basis of national unity in this country and which give every Canadian in every part of this country a fair shake regardless of place of residence. The criterion for eligibility for these programs is simply being Canadian. Now the federal Tories, based on their ideology, have .begun to tinker with these programs so that Canadians cannot access them equally, depending on where they live in the country, on income, and other things.
All of these national institutions, whether based on social programs or on national institutions and symbols such as the CBC, the communications system, the rail transportation system, or the Canada Post system, are being undermined. Canadians are losing a fundamental understanding of what really underlies this nation, something we have treasured over the last 125 years.
There is one national symbol of Canada that is recognized all across this country and all around the world. That symbol is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which was established as the North-West Mounted Police in the 1870s. That police force was a federal police force which was designed to bring law and order and orderly development to the west at a time when Canadians were viewing the chaos taking place in the United States. Canadians felt that a police force was necessary to bring good government, law and order, and good policing to western Canada. The North-West Mounted Police later became the national police of

Canada and the police force in many of the provinces and municipalities of Canada; a great deal of respect has accrued to that police force both in the country and around the world.
It is very difficult to identify any other symbol which might be more representative of Canada than the red serge uniform of the RCMP. When somebody comes to the Canadian capital they have their picture taken with an RCMP officer in the dress uniform.
In provincial capitals they do the same thing. In citizenship court one of the symbols of Canada that is evident along with the flag and the coats of arms is the red serge uniform of the RCMP. It is seen as a symbol of Canada both nationally and internationally.
In renegotiating the terms of the contracts with the provinces which use the RCMP in their municipalities, the Solicitor General and the Government of Canada are taking an intransigent position in demanding that the municipalities and provinces pay a higher share of the cost. In doing so, the federal government is putting even the institution of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in jeopardy.
What it is telling the provinces and municipalities which contract for those RCMP services is that it is going to raise the price so high and make policing such a burden on the taxpayers that there is now an option. They can create their own municipal police force or provincial police force and the federal government will get out of that area of policing entirely.
There are going to be serious repercussions across Canada in terms of national unity and in terms of recognition of the symbols and institutions of this country if the government proceeds in its hard-nosed intransigent stance in dealing with the Canadian provinces and municipalities which contract for RCMP services.
One of the major contractors for the services of the RCMP is the province of British Columbia, the province from which I come. According to the Union of B.C.
Municipalities, which has put together substantial research on this issue, 27 per cent of the RCMP force in Canada is in B.C.; out of 15,000 RCMP members 4,000 are posted to British Columbia.
The province of British Columbia is also a major contractor for Royal Canadian Mounted Police services. Out of 8,000 contracting RCMP members, 3,100 of those are posted in British Columbia. Thirty-nine per cent of all the contracted provincial police services through the RCMP are contracted within that province. That same thing applies to members of the RCMP who are contracted at the provincial level.
This is a very important issue for municipalities within the province of British Columbia because they employ 1,900 out of the 3,000 RCMP members contracted to municipalities across Canada. That is, 63 per cent of all the members of the force who are contracted to municipalities work in the municipalities of British Columbia, serving close to a million and a half British Columbians.
This is a very important issue in British Columbia. I do not want to understate how important it is in western Canada as well. The RCMP has been the traditional police force in western Canada since the North-West Mounted Police originated in the 1870s.
We are concerned about the effect on British Columbia. Municipalities have advised us that if the federal government persists with its intransigent position in RCMP contract negotiations, it is going to cost the municipalities of that province an additional $12.5 million annually to support the RCMP. That translates over the 10-year term of the contract into an additional $125 million being bled out of those municipalities to support police services.
In the case of the government of the province of British Columbia which contracts to the RCMP for its provincial police, it means an additional $27 million a year to a government which has just budgeted a $395 million deficit.
May 24, 1991

We are talking about a province unable to pay those kinds of increases and municipalities within that province which are unable to pass on those kinds of increases to their taxpayers without creating a serious burden. It will be a burden on taxpayers which in addition to other federal taxes such as excise taxes, fuel taxes, goods and services taxes, increased income taxes, increased charges for all federal services, and another tax increase passed on to municipal property owners and residents as a result of the policing contracts with the federal government is going to be absolutely impossible to bear. These costs run so high for municipalities in British Columbia right now-some municipalities pay up to 37 per cent of their revenues for policing costs-that there may be no legal avenue for them to pass those costs on to property taxes.
What we are talking about here is another element of Conservative policy that is involved in this debate: the aspect of constantly increasing taxes on the lower and middle classes in this country which are being expected to support these kinds of services when the federal government is fully capable of providing services at the current cost-sharing level.
I just wanted to mention some of the impacts on municipalities within my riding, and I will quote from some of the mayors in the riding of Comox-Albemi. For example, Mayor Ron Webber of Courtenay, British Columbia, has said that over the past years the presence of the RCMP has provided a cost effective and efficient method of providing total policing for federal and municipal responsibilities.
It is also an important factor in maintaining a federal presence in our community and contributes greatly to preserving a sense of national identity in these threatened times.
The increase proposed by the federal government represents a 17.35 per cent increase in a single year and would result in a 5.4 per cent increase in municipal property tax rates.
It should also be pointed out that this analysis is based on the city's fiscal year, which is the calendar year, and that the impact of the federal proposal for a full fiscal year at the new tax rates would result in a 25 per cent
Supply
increase in the cost of policing services for that small municipality and a 7.8 per cent increase in tax rates.
For communities like Courtenay, British Columbia, a 25 per cent increase in policing costs and a 7.8 per cent increase in taxing based on those costs and on the federal contract proposal are simply far too much for those municipalities and those taxpayers to bear.
As a result, they are going to be forced into a position either of cutting back on police services at a time when we are reading in The Ottawa Citizen that women in communities such as Ottawa are fearful of going out at night in their own neighbourhoods because of danger to their physical well-being.
Now is not the time to start cutting back on RCMP services or on the fairness of cost distribution among the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities.
Now is the time for the federal, provincial, and municipal governments to be maintaining and improving services. It is time for the federal government to accept its share of the responsibility so that men and women in our communities across Canada can feel safe going out at night in their neighbourhoods.
Now is not the time to start pushing this kind of contract proposal on to the provinces and municipalities in western Canada. Now is the time when they can least afford to bear it.
I would also like to quote the mayor of Port Albemi, the city where I live. He says: "A prime example of the federal benefit of municipal policing is their front line enforcement against dmg offences. This is an area of federal policing responsibility which is handled on a more cost effective basis by contract police forces. If it were not for municipal contracts, the cost to the federal government would most assuredly be increased".
The mayor of Port Albemi and I do not always agree, but in this case we are absolutely in agreement.
If the federal government persists in its intransigent position with respect to increasing costs to the province and the municipalities within the province of British Columbia, it is going to persuade some of those municipalities to go to municipal police forces.

May 24, 1991
Supply
It may persuade the province to go to a provincial police force, and we are going to end up with the kind of balkanized police jurisdiction where the transfer of information either slows down or does not exist.
We are going to have a situation similar to that in the United States where they have local police, county police, state police and the national police force, the FBI. Information transfer between those police agencies is often extremely difficult, if it exists at all.
There is often a confusion over jurisdiction on issues which are seen to be federal, state, local or county. As a result, police services in the United States often break down and do not perform as effectively as they should.
I do not think that there is anyone in Canada or around the world who is not aware of the effectiveness of the RCMP as a national police force, a provincial police force, and as a municipal police force.
Part of the reason for the effectiveness of that force is that it is able to integrate its services at all three levels of government. Its communications systems operate between the three levels of government and for that reason it is far more effective.
I hope that members in this House will support the resolution that I have put forward, will do their best to persuade the Solicitor General and the Government of Canada that the cost base of the RCMP contract in western Canada is appropriate, that we should not be trying to force increases in the provincial or the municipalities' share, and that the federal government should be accepting its full responsibility. If not, the result, as I have pointed out, is to jeopardize national unity. The result will further increase the tax burden on the provinces and the municipalities, while at the same time reduce the effectiveness of policing at the very time in Canada when we would like to increase the security and the safety of our citizens, at the very time in Canada when people are beginning to be afraid to go out in their own neighbourhoods.
I urge members to support this resolution. I also urge the Solicitor General to support this resolution and get down to the business of negotiating, in good faith, with
the western provinces and the municipalities that contract with the federal government for RCMP services.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am absolutely astounded that the member from lotus land wants other Canadian taxpayers to subsidize policing services in British Columbia.
British Columbia has an economy that is doing better than any other province in the country. Right now, for example, in Ontario we are having a very difficult time. I find it very odd that the member should be demanding that we pay for his province's policing services.
The RCMP can certainly stay there, but British Columbia should pay the cost of its own policing. Local control means that we have local funding for the level of policing that we want in our community. That should not be paid for by other Canadian taxpayers.
Certainly national unity is not dependent on subsidies.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think if the member had any understanding or experience of British Columbia at all, instead of insulting it by calling it lotus land, she would know that in communities like mine we have just lost over 400 jobs in the plywood industry. There is some question as to whether some of those communities in western Canada are going to survive. Much of the losses are a result of Tory trade policy.
Perhaps the hon. member should spend a little more time in British Columbia to learn exactly how much British Columbia contributes, not simply to its own economy, but to the economy of Canada as a whole.
We are very proud, as British Columbians, that we have never stinted in providing the revenue from our resources and the income taxes and other taxes that hard-working British Columbians pay. We pay our share, and more.
What we are asking in terms of police services is that we get a little bit of that back. We are not asking for the whole amount back. We are asking that we get a little bit of the revenues that we pay to the federal government back in order to provide a decent standard of police services in the province of British Columbia.
May 24, 1991

I can tell the hon. member that British Columbians are not going to receive very well the insult of that Tory member calling British Columbia lotus land.

Madam Speaker, I could hardly believe my ears when I heard the member for Don Valley North insult the three million Canadians who live in British Columbia by calling it lotus land. The member should visit the province.
I finally discovered this morning what those opposite are trying to do. The Prime Minister is trying to get the Republican nomination for vice-president in the next election. How is he trying to do it? He is trying to turn Toronto, Vancouver, Ottawa and every city within driving distance of the border into shopping suburbs of New York, Buffalo and places like that. In the case of the member's constituency, he is trying to turn Toronto into a shopping suburb of Buffalo.
Where has the hon. member been. Does she not realize that 400,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost in Ontario in the last 18 months? Where has she been for the last 18 months?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday the Royal Canadian Mounted Police celebrated its birthday. In 1873, the North-West Mounted Police was founded. It was later to become known as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The RCMP, as was indicated, is an important national symbol for Canadians. It is one of the most important national symbols that we have in Canada.

May 24, 1991
Supply
People world wide know about the RCMP. In fact, they make movies in Hollywood about the RCMP and the work of the RCMP. It is well known that the RCMP always gets their person.
The federal government is now bent on wiping out the RCMP in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada. At present, the RCMP acts as the provincial police force in eight of the 10 provinces and in the two territories. The federal government also contracts the RCMP to municipalities in those eight provinces.
In the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, there are provincial police forces. In the province of Ontario we have the OPP and in Quebec the Surete du Quebec. Those of us who reside and have our constituencies in Ontario and Quebec do not realize how important the RCMP is to western Canada and to western Canadians.
Over the last number of months, in fact over the last year, the government has been negotiating a new contract, and has acted in bad faith. The old contract expired on March 31 of this year. The present Solicitor General is sitting in the House today. He is responsible for negotiating this new contract with the provinces to ensure that the RCMP continue to provide the important and essential services it provides in western and Atlantic Canada.

speechtext: He is also an Ontario member.

That previous contract expired and the government, in advance of the expiration of that previous contract, said it was not prepared to bend at all regarding the proposal it had put forward to renegotiate the contract. This is a new 10-year contract that will see the relationship continue from this year until the year 2001.
The contract expired and the contract services continue, but under no contract. The government has been totally intransigent in terms of negotiating in good faith.
At present the federal government pays 30 per cent of the cost of those services in western Canada. The member for North York should know that the provinces and municipalities in western Canada pay the lion's share, 70 per cent, of the cost of RCMP services in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada.
The government is proposing to cut the federal share to 25 per cent. As well, the Government of Canada, through the Solicitor General, wants to impose additional administrative costs on the municipalities and the provincial governments. That will mean an additional cut of $79 million from the federal government. At present the federal, government's share is some $251 million.
It is my view that these cuts are part of a systematic and deliberate program to dismember and destroy our country and the national symbols that exist in Canada that promote national identity and Canadianism. In seven short years-long years to a lot of us on this side of the House-this government has systematically cut institutions right across the board. It started by dismantling FIRA, the Foreign Investment Review Agency. It is privatizing Petro-Canada. It has privatized Air Canada. It is in the process of privatizing Harbourfront in metropolitan Toronto. It has cut the CBC. It is cutting Canada Post. It has destroyed VIA Rail and now is bent on destroying the RCMP in western Canada.
What is the agenda? I believe that is a fair question to ask.

My friend from Alberta says that the Prime Minister wants to run for vice-president of the United States.
The cynics among us would tend to agree that the government's agenda includes the gradual disintegration of our country and integration into the United States.
Municipalities will be hard hit by these proposals of the federal government. In effect, what the federal government is trying to do is reduce the deficit on the backs of municipalities in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada. They are trying to off-load expenses, in this case $79 million this year.
When you consider the importance and the benefit of the RCMP in western Canada, it really makes you wonder about the government's priorities. It seems to be able to find money, left and right, to accommodate the friends of the Tory government, friends of the Prime Minister, and friends of cabinet ministers, giving them all kinds of untendered contracts. The government is paying legal fees for Sinclair Stevens, $500,000, and $5 million to conduct a royal commission of inquiry into the conduct of a former Conservative cabinet minister who was found to be in breach 17 or 18 times over of the conflict of interest guidelines.
May 24, 1991

The government seems to be able to find money when it comes to accommodating its own interests. But when it comes to dealing with some important matters that face Canadians, it does not seem to be able to find the necessary resources. Is it any wonder that western Canadians sense this growing alienation when people from central Canada, the Conservative Party, and Conservative members like the hon. member for North York speak the way they do, showing a total lack of understanding and a total ignorance of what is happening in western Canada?
Here we have the Solicitor General from Ontario, Orillia of all places, acting in bad faith in negotiating this new contract. What will the federal cuts actually mean to the various provinces that are affected? In the province of British Columbia the extra cost will be $120 million over the 10-year period of this contract. In the province of Alberta the extra cost will be $15 million. In fact, municipalities within the province of Alberta are considering establishing their own police forces. In the city of Red Deer, for example, the additional cost has led municipal leaders there to seriously consider establishing their own police force, thereby eliminating the presence of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In the province of Saskatchewan, in the town of Rosthern, they are considering establishing their own police force in view of the proposals of the federal government.
In the province of Manitoba the federal proposal will mean an additional $90 million over the life of the contract.
In Nova Scotia the federal proposal will mean that the municipalities in the province will have to pay 23 per cent more in the first year of the new contract, $9 million more annually.
The province of New Brunswick, which became fed up with federal irresponsibility in this area some time ago, established its own highway patrol, thereby taking that responsibility away from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There, too, the province suffered substantially.
It has gone back to the RCMP because it believes the force provides an excellent service. The RCMP is highly respected right across the country. It is one of the most respected police forces anywhere in the world and, if this

government has its way, it will systematically slash and cut and destroy the RCMP in western Canada.
We know that this arrangement, negotiated by the previous government, in which the RCMP contracts its services to the provinces in western Canada and to municipalities, results in a significant cost saving for taxpayers. For example, in the province of Quebec the per capita cost for policing is $170. In Ontario that cost is $155. That includes, of course, all the various police forces that exist in the two provinces. In the municipality that I represent we have the Metropolitan Toronto Police, the Ontario Provincial Police and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, all providing police services.
The cost in B.C. to provide police services is $127 per capita. From $170 in Quebec, $155 in Ontario, to $127 in British Columbia, you can see, Madam Speaker, the significant cost saving for this arrangement.
The member for North York would have people believe, or is suggesting that the benefit is only to the provinces in question, that the provinces and municipalities which contract for these services are benefiting, and that the fat cats in Ontario and Quebec are in effect footing the bill or paying the cost of policing in those particular provinces and municipalities.
The member forgets that there is significant benefit to the federal government and to the federal taxpayer with this particular arrangement, remembering of course that the federal government is only paying 30 per cent of the cost and that there are federal taxpayers in the western provinces who pay their taxes to Ottawa every April and from every pay.
What are the benefits to the federal government, to the national government? We have spoken about the visible national symbol. We cannot attach a price tag to that in terms of the benefit to Canadians. We have a national police force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The men and women who serve Canada well are seen as an international symbol.
When you are in western Canada and you see the RCMP, you see Canada. You see security. You see a highly respected police officer who works hard and diligently on the part of Canadians. Wherever you travel in western Canada, you see that national presence.

May 24, 1991

The RCMP is one of the few institutions in Canada that provides that national presence. We have Petro-Canada stations across the country. We have Air Canada across the country. But the RCMP comes into contact day in and day out with people, providing that service.
If the federal government had its way, as you travelled through western Canada you would see a separate police force in Calgary, a separate police force in Lethbridge, a separate police force in Red Deer, a separate police force in Vancouver and another police force in North Vancouver. There would be all kinds of separate police forces in the municipalities, separate provincial police forces in the four western provinces and the provinces in Atlantic Canada, the Northwest Territories and Yukon.

speechtext: That is nation building.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
My friend and colleague says "nation building". He is absolutely right, because from 1873 to the present moment the RCMP and its predecessor, the North-West Mounted Police, helped build this nation, helped provide the symbols of importance to our country.
That is a significant benefit to the federal government. For a mere $270-odd million a year the cost is well worth it. As well, there is one single police structure in western Canada as opposed to having a separate RCMP detachment, a separate OPP detachment, and a separate office for the Metropolitan Toronto Police for example. There is one single structure that allows the government to save significantly in terms of its responsibilities in enforcing federal laws. The RCMP, the federal police, whether or not we like it, will still have a role to play if the provinces in western Canada provincialize their police forces and the municipalities go with their own police forces. We still need the RCMP to enforce federal drug laws, for example.
If we have that duplication of service, we will not have the uniformed RCMP any longer. We will have the undercover RCMP officers as we have in Quebec and Ontario investigating drug deals and drug trafficking, for example.
There are significant savings to the federal taxpayers when we have a single policing structure. Let us make sure that the wrong impression is not left with Canadians
that somehow central Canadians are paying for policing in western Canada and are not receiving any benefit in return.
Western Canadians are Canadians. They are federal taxpayers and they are contributing to the federal coffers distributed from here. You do not see western Canadians or Atlantic Canadians complaining when federal funds are used for massive expenditures in the province of Ontario or in the province of Quebec.
It really surprises me that a Conservative member would begrudge giving western Canadians the moneys necessary to ensure the continuation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in western Canada.
It is clear that this government simply does not care about the continuation of the RCMP. It is attempting to shift the tax burden in an irresponsible fashion on to the municipalities.
We know that the federal government is seriously affecting the universality of health care throughout the country by trying to off-load some of the federal costs on to the provinces. In effect, health services are already suffering because of the massive cutbacks of this government.
In education as well, the government has severely cut back in terms of federal transfer payments to the municipalities. Education is suffering and now policing will suffer in a very significant way.
What is encouraging is that the eight provinces and the territories which are affected are standing together shoulder to shoulder and they are fighting this. They are fed up with it and they are not going to put up with it. They are not prepared to bend over and die as the federal Solicitor General hopes they will. They are adamant that they will not be forced into paying the substantial additional costs.
The provincial solicitors general have met over the last number of months and their position remains firm. They will not send the additional moneys to the federal government. The ball will then be in the federal court.
Will the Solicitor General, perhaps when he gets up in a few minutes, indicate his intentions in so far as this particular matter is concerned? Does he intend to unilaterally pull the RCMP from western Canada or Atlantic Canada? Is he prepared to negotiate in good faith?


May 24, 1991

The deal that was struck 10 years ago was a good deal. It was a fair deal. Why then would the government now want to change that relationship which has worked so well over the last 10 years and in the many years before that?
One can understand that both levels of government will have to pay the additional cost in terms of inflation and other associated costs of providing policing, but why, pray tell, does the federal government want to off-load or renegotiate this particular agreement in such an unfair fashion?
The provincial governments are sticking together. They do not appreciate the federal government's take-it-or-leave-it attitude. They are prepared to call the Solicitor General's bluff and say: "We will continue to pay our fair share when we write the check every month or every two months. We will write a check according to the old formula".
Then it will be up to the federal government and the Solicitor General to decide what the next step is in terms of trying to further their unfair proposal. I have indicated in my submissions the reasons why I believe the federal government should continue to pay its fair share.
Has my time expired, Madam Speaker?

The Liberal Party fully, completely and unequivocally supports the continuation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in western Canada, in Atlantic Canada and in the territories. When we get on the other side of the House we will ensure the presence of the RCMP in western Canada.

First of all I want to thank my colleague for his comprehensive analysis of this particular problem. I particularly appreciated the comments with respect to our proud force, the RCMP, in its efficiency as a policing unit and its importance as a national symbol, particularly for western and northern Canadians.

There are two questions which I would like to raise. I want to make certain that all members recognize that when we say this is another attack on a bond, a national symbol that contributes to the unification of Canada, it is understood that this is not only being said by Liberals and other members on this side of the House. I have a quote here from Minister McCrae from the province of Manitoba who is a member of the Conservative government there: "At a time of great stress on our country it would be a tragedy if short-sighted federal fiscal policies snapped another bond that unifies this country".
Does my colleague know of any other individuals who have made similar observations?
The other question is with respect to the cost that would be off-loaded to provinces. He did mention those. I think they are particularly important and assuming that he can reach them without a whole lot of difficulty I would like to have those repeated for Canadians who are listening because they do represent an additional major burden on provinces and municipalities. That is one of the ways the federal government is able to say it is controlling its expenditures at 3.7 per cent. Obviously it is. It is dumping it on to the provinces and the municipalities.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
At present the federal government's share of RCMP contract policing is $251.7 million. The proposal put forward by the federal government would see that particular share cut by $79 million.
You simply cannot cut $79 million and hope that the cost disappears somehow. That cost will have to be borne by provinces and municipalities. Municipal taxpayers will bear the brunt of this increase. That is a significant amount of money for municipalities when you break it down on a city-by-city, town-by-town basis across western and northern Canada and in Atlantic Canada.
As far as the question relating to the other people who have commented about the disintegration of Canada and the destruction of national symbols, particularly the destruction and dismembering of the RCMP, many Canadians right across Canada revere and highly respect the RCMP and have been shocked to learn of the hidden agenda of this government: to destroy the RCMP throughout Canada.

May 24, 1991

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
I find it extremely interesting that the member for York South- Weston is suggesting that his taxpayers, who are paying not just the $155 Ontario average cost for policing but a substantially higher figure because it is metropolitan Toronto, should in fact be subsidizing communities in provinces such as British Columbia which have policing costs of $127 per capita, on which they are getting a further subsidy of 30 per cent. It seems to me that they are paying in some areas of British Columbia around $89 for policing.
In metropolitan Toronto many people have great difficulty paying their very high property taxes and living in one of the most expensive cities in North America. It seems to me that while hon. members are trying to turn this into an issue by suggesting that the RCMP should disappear, it really is an issue of fiscal fairness. Nobody is suggesting the RCMP disappear. We are suggesting that communities pay their own costs of policing and determine the level of policing services they require.
For the information of some of the other members, I have visited all parts-

It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to Members' Statements, pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, the removal of interprovincial trade barriers as a means to stimulate economic growth from within Canada was one of the central themes in the government's Speech from the Throne.
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island moved one step closer to that goal yesterday when the Council of Maritime Premiers released their discussion paper calling for the removal of a number of
interprovincial trade barriers over the next 18 months. Citing the fact that the three provinces are too small to put up walls, the premiers outline a number of areas in which economic integration can begin, including the free movement between provinces for professionals and trades people and the elimination of costly bidding wars used to attract businesses into a particular province.
It is high time the rest of the country took the lead from the three maritime premiers and began working to remove the over 500 interprovincial trade barriers that are currently choking economic growth in Canada.

Madam Speaker, today, on Sneaker Day, all Canadians are invited and urged to wear their running shoes and show their support for a healthy and active life style. Sneaker Day kicks off Canada Fitness Week which starts today and will continue until June 2. Canada Fitness Week has now been recognized internationally as the biggest celebration of physical fitness in the world. This year, more than 8 million Canadians are expected to take part in some
14,000	activities that will take place across this country. In our communities, hundred of thousands of volunteers will donate their time and energy to this annual celebration.
During the next nine days, I invite all members to join Canadians from coast to coast in promoting and taking part in the many activities scheduled during Canada Fitness Week.

Madam Speaker, the Self-Employment Incentive Program of Canada Employment and Immigration has proven to be the best economic development tool available in my area.
Under SEI, unemployed people are provided incentives to start their own small businesses and get off unemployment insurance benefits. To date there are over 150 participants who are operating their own small businesses and in some cases already employing others.
May 24, 1991

Not only is SEI successful in helping people get off UIC, but it is providing a foundation of new business experience and fostering a new entrepreneurial spirit.
Cumberland county enjoys perhaps the very best success rate in Canada under the SEI program. It is so successful, in fact, that funding for 1991 is now exhausted. If Cumberland county is to continue their success rate, we need the budget to continue this program. I know of no other government program which provides better value and I strongly urge the minister to reassess this situation and provide the additional funding required.

Madam Speaker, last week the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced $7 million in funding for small craft harbours. I stand in this House today and ask that some of that money be spent in the Cardigan riding.
Since the 1988 election I have written countless letters asking that repairs be done to the wharfs in eastern Prince Edward Island. I know of two wharfs in eastern Prince Edward Island that needed approximately $50,000 in repairs last spring. Because these repairs were not done, the cost to the taxpayer today is about $1.5 million.
However, the government commitment is only to minor harbour maintenance. Cardigan riding could probably use the $7 million itself, because the government did not perform the minor harbour maintenance in the past.
The minister should act today and help the fishermen of Cardigan riding.

Madam Speaker, six months ago I wrote the then Minister of Employment and Immigration about discriminatory hiring practices on the international bridge between Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, and Michigan. This bridge is a jointly owned and operated bridge with supposed equal interest between the United States and Canada.
A 30-year old agreement between the two countries designating a 50-50 worker ratio is being denied by the American government. Presently 25 Americans and 18 Canadians are working at various tasks on the bridge. Why the discrepancy you ask? Why, after six months, is there no answer? Why is the prepared answer being reconsidered by the new minister?
It would appear that not only the playing field is tilted in favour of the Americans, but also the working field.
I have not received a written response to my letter, but I have been told that once again the infamous FTA, free trade agreement, has struck down Canadian workers. Chapter 15, which appears totally irrelevant, impedes Canadians from an equal employment opportunity on this bridge.
We are meeting this summer to resolve this inequity. Let us hope this government will be strong in its resolve to correct this obvious inequity.

Madam Speaker, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms enshrines in our Constitution the principle of multiculturalism which promotes respect for cultural and linguistic origins of all Canadians, encourages Canadians to get to know and understand each other, and ensures that all Canadians of whatever origin can and must participate equally and fully in the wider Canadian society.
Multiculturalism has come under fire from two different sources. The Citizens' Forum on Canada's Future says that many Canadians reject government funding for multicultural programs and believe that new Canadians should embrace our symbols, our culture, and our definition of what it means to be a Canadian.
On the other hand, the Quebec Belanger-Campeau report says that multiculturalism implies the equality of all cultures and cultural origins in Canada and thus conflicts with the concept of two founding nations.
Surely we can find a way to reconcile all of these views and principles without disregarding any of them. In the past, we have emphasized our differences. Now it is time to emphasize the things that make us all Canadians. Certainly we have more-

May 24, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unfortunately, the hon. member's time has expired.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the news media report that IVACO of Marieville, Quebec, which operates steel mills in several Canadian towns and cities, including L'Orignal, Ontario, in my riding, is preparing to relocate part of its operations to the United States.
Why? Because, according to IVACO's president, Paul Ivanier, the Canadian dollar is now artificially high. Mr. Ivanier says that he thinks the Canadian dollar should be worth 80 cents U.S.
Madam Speaker, we in the Liberal Party have told the government for a long time that its monetary and fiscal policies were driving away investors and encouraging business operators to transfer jobs to the United States.
The Hon. Leader of the Opposition has asked the Canadian government several times to lower the value of our dollar so that we can keep our jobs in Canada. Why does the government opposite refuse to act? Why does it refuse to protect these jobs?

Madam Speaker, the Reform Party uses the words "phased reduction and elimination of all agricultural subsidies and support programs".
There are no countries in the western democratic world which do not support its agricultural producers. The farmers of Canada have contributed to the growth and prosperity of this great land. The minimum support which our government has contributed during drought, flood, and low world prices has kept in excess of 100,000 farmers from abandoning their livelihood, production, and contribution to Canada.
This Conservative government will continue support programs to ensure the survival of farmers, while the Reform Party will eliminate programs and farmers.
Preston Manning is now saying that by eliminating farm program assistance and elimination of the Crow benefit, the government can reduce the national debt.
This Conservative government has no intention of reducing the national debt on the back of farmers. That hare-brained idea we will leave to the Reform Party and Preston Manning.

Madam Speaker, the RCMP recently reported that there are almost one million restricted weapons in Canada. Last year, more than 45,000 new restricted weapons were registered. Only four were refused. We have no idea how many guns there are in Canada because non-restricted weapons, such as the semi-automatic that killed 14 young women in Montreal, are not registered anywhere. Children have shot each other and themselves with legal weapons. In my community of Burnaby we have seen the horror of a random, drive-by shooting.
I have called on this government to bring in effective gun control legislation. They have ignored this and with Bill C-6 they have gone right off the deep end. It encourages the manufacture and export of automatic weapons.
The empty rhetoric of this government in damning the gun trade during the Persian Gulf crisis rings very hollow. When it delayed gun control legislation before, Canadians thought it was weak-kneed and ignorant of the issue. Now the government has proved it.

Madam Speaker, I rise today in support of the creation of a computerized national emergency response information system which will enable firefighters and other authorities to obtain accurate instant information at the scene of a hazardous materials incident.
Technologically advanced systems are available which not only aid in identifying what hazardous materials are present but offer detailed information on appropriate emergency response techniques.

I join the International Association of Firefighters and urge this government to consider seriously the implementation of such a national emergency system.

Madam Speaker, more than 50 years ago, a group of men and women in the Montreal area founded the first Optimist Club of Quebec. Today, with more than 40,000 members organized in 760 clubs, Quebec has the highest concentration of Optimists in North America. This enthusiasm is even more remarkable when we consider that the sole purpose of the world's 4,000 Optimist Clubs is community service.
Last year, 4 million young people were able to take advantage of programs offered by Optimist International. The wide range of programs offered by the Optimists includes drug awareness programs for young people and programs designed to help children who are disadvantaged or disabled. This kind of involvement in our communities, Madam Speaker, is essential to our wellbeing, and I urge all Canadians to support the efforts of Optimist International.
Madam Speaker, in concluding I want to congratulate the Chairman of Optimist International, Dr. Tate Thigpen of Jackson, Mississipi, and his colleagues, all of whom are here today, as they are having their annual meeting here in Ottawa.

Madam Speaker, the people of Bangladesh continue to suffer from the devastating effects of a cyclone that has ravaged their country. Already there are over 125,000 confirmed deaths and estimates that the number may increase to as many as 500,000.
As is too often the case, the poorest portion of the population is suffering the most. The Canadian government, through its development agency, has contributed emergency aid to help relieve this suffering and it is undoubtedly helping in the short term.
My concern lies in what happens in the long term. Lack of equitable land distribution in a country dependent on agriculture is the root cause of the increasing poverty level in Bangladesh. It is this problem which is forcing people to migrate to the coastal areas, the first and most severely affected regions when the cyclone winds start to blow.
In a country where 10 per cent of the population owns 50 per cent of the land, the poorest farmers are left with little choice and less opportunity. They can either rent land from absentee landlords or they can move to the coastal areas where they might have a chance to own land. It is these coastal areas which become danger zones when the winds arrive. It is these poor migrant farmers who-

The hon. member for Chambly.

Madam Speaker, I rise to urge this government to stop the post office closures that are occurring all over Canada, including in my riding of Chambly. To date over 950 federally owned and operated post offices have been closed or privatized. By July over 150 more post offices are scheduled to be closed.
How can this government justify taking away reliable postal services from Canadians? The government takes great pride in offering a Decima poll which says 91 per cent of the people who have privatized service are satisfied.
If this is such a reliable poll, why will the corporation not allow the municipalities to decide if their post offices should be closed. The hundreds of letters I have from residents of Mabou, Nova Scotia, the rally staged by residents of Avonmore, Ontario, yesterday on the steps of Parliament, and the court challenge launched against Canada Post by Rejean Lemare of La Redemption, Quebec, on Wednesday do not suggest a 91 per cent approval rating.
I urge this government to stop talking down to Canadians. This government must stop-
May 24, 1991

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, but time is up. The hon. member for Lotbiniere.

Madam Speaker, I would like to talk about an organization in my riding called the Centre d'initiative d'emploi de Lotbiniere-Ouest (CIEL), which was created in 1985 further to a job development program for ten municipalities in the riding that have a total population of about 15,000.
This organization makes up for the deficiencies in the banking system and reaches those who are often unreached. It is non-profit and depends on its 270 member subscribers who deposit from $30 to $2,000 in a fund. In addition, the local Caisses Populaires contribute substantially to this fund.
Since it was founded, the organization has helped more than 31 local businesses with interest-free loans totaling some $46,325 and has managed to maintain and often to create jobs.
Madam Speaker, that is an example of people who have taken charge of their affairs and have confidence in one another.
I congratulate Rolland Paradis and his team on having set up such an organization for the greater good of our community.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Finance or the Acting Minister of Finance.
Yesterday in the House the minister admitted that the economy had hit rock bottom. Today numbers released by the government confirm that for many people there is
no hope for an early recovery because they have gone bankrupt. Over-all bankruptcies are up by 77 per cent.
When will the government admit that the policies of the previous Minister of Finance are bankrupt. And when will the new Minister of Finance take his responsibility and introduce the new budget, something that Canada needs very badly at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think all Canadians know that Canada has been going through a recession.
I would like to remind the hon. Leader of the Opposition that in our 1989 and 1990 budgets, we warned Canadians that demand was far too high, that they were overspending and putting themselves at risk. We are now in the midst of a recession, but fortunately-these are numbers from last month-there are many signs that we are beginning to extricate ourselves from this. One of them is the bank rate which went down again yesterday.
Interest rates have gone down 5 per cent in a few months. This is quite an achievement compared to the Liberal record of high interest rates in the 1980s.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this government jacked up the interest rates four or five points above the Americans; now, rates go down a bit, and it takes credit. If it had not made mistakes some years ago it would not be able to take credit for anything at this moment. The results are there. This budget was the wrong budget at the wrong time. I can see the former Minister of Finance regretting now what he has done. What are the results today?

The results are that in Ontario, personal bankruptcies have risen 123 per cent; in British Columbia, 109 per cent; in Alberta, the present finance minister's province, 96 per cent.
So when will the government realize that its economic policies have been tragic for very many Canadians and when will it act to stimulate the economy and not impose policies that just slow down the economy and create more bankruptcies every day?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition just said that we had forced interest rates up artificially, according to him.
May 24, 1991

I would say to him that interest rates were so high because of the disastrous debt that the Liberal administration left us. When we showed in our budget that we were determined to solve the government's financial problem, interest rates started to go down. It is precisely by creating such conditions without backing away or letting interest rates rise to 22 per cent, as the Liberals did, that we are bringing them down to their lowest level in three years.
Everywhere we see signs of the new R-word, "recovery"; we see indications that at last Canada is getting ready to enjoy several years of great prosperity, as we did before under this Conservative government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in this morning's papers, the president of IVACO said that what was hurting the economy was the fact that interest rates were higher than in the United States and that the government maintained the dollar at artificially high levels which made it hard for Canadian products to be competitive. When will the government realize its mistakes, ensure interest rates are more competitive than they have been during the past four years, and bring the Canadian dollar back to levels that will help our exports since our economy depends to a very considerable extent on exports? Why not let the dollar go down so that manufacturers can stay in business and not go bankrupt?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope God will protect us from Liberal solutions which have proved extremely costly for Canada. We cannot run away from our problems. Canada must meet these problems head on. And that is what we are doing. If we consider one particular sector or group that has been severely affected, the manufacturing sector for instance-I suggest we listen to what was said by the chairman of this group yesterday in committee in response to the Liberal industrial critic, Mr. Peterson, the hon. member for Willowdale. Mr. Thibault said the following and I will quote him in English:

"Many of the policies touted by Peterson would force the federal government to increase its spending and that would only make the current economic mess worse. The
Oral Questions
result would be higher taxes, a larger deficit, and higher taxes".

Madam Speaker, I must say that the only proposal we have had from the other side of the House regarding every single policy we have adopted is this: spend more. That is not the answer, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Finance). What will the minister do to help Canadian retailers who are threatened with bankruptcy as a result of losing $100 million annually to American stores across the border?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I pointed out yesterday, we have embarked on a nation-wide consultative process with the hope of taking some immediate steps to alleviate this very complex problem which spans all three levels of government and includes problems associated with the private sector, labour, as well as consumer organizations. We are well on our way to making some definitive suggestions to what all of these stakeholders together should and must take.
As far as the customs operations are concerned, we have begun to put into place more efficient and effective ways of collecting applicable duties and taxes. Although border crossings have increased by some 20 per cent, 23 per cent last month for example, our customs collections have increased by well over 150 per cent. Action is being taken at the border, but this is a much broader problem which comes down to the fact that Canadians are not as competitive as their American counterparts.
I think that the Speech from the Throne addressed that in a very positive manner. This government has taken and will continue to take action to make it possible for Canadian businesses to become more competitive.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of National Revenue who clearly has not implemented any new policies.

May 24, 1991
Oral Questions
Thirty-three tax increases in seven years have driven Canadians south to shop. Mobs of Canadians at our customs offices have slowed the entry of American residents to this country to a trickle.
Will the minister take immediate steps to designate a special line for Americans at our border crossings so that Canadians can profit from American visits to Canada to help offset the government's persistent inaction and blundering?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is totally misinformed when he says that we have not taken any action at the border. Through our Customs 2000 program we have initiated a variety of proposals too numerous to mention today: automated cash registers and use of new technology including electronic data interchange and pre-clearance of commercial traffic, more efficient use of staff, special express lanes, PACE project and so on.
At customs operations, we have to perform a fine balancing act from, on the one side, collecting duties and taxes more effectively and efficiently while at the same time relieving congestion at the border which would allow tourism and commercial traffic to come in. We are trying to perform that balancing act.
I have made a commitment to each community that we will develop tailor-made projects for those communities, which we have put in in many places. We are willing and anxious to co-operate with each community and we are meeting with the mayors in the communities involved.
I know where this government is going and what this government is doing. I would like to know if the Liberal Party wants the borders to be wide open or wants the borders to be totally closed? Let us know where the Liberal Party stands because we know where we stand.

Madam Speaker, my question is on the record increase in bankruptcies which has hit this country.
Yesterday, there was brave talk from the government about the fact that we were into a recovery. Today the harsh reality is there of this 77 per cent increase in bankruptcies.

There were nearly 7,000 bankruptcies in April, 77 per cent more than last April. Will the minister keep pretending that all is well? Or is this government finally prepared to do something for Canadians and take steps to end this recession?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member may wish to check what he said. In quoting a figure he referred to millions which is not correct. It was probably an oversight.
That being said, I do not deny we have been through difficult times. However, we are talking about figures that are now behind us and we have good reason to look to the future.
The hon. member asked when we would start doing something for Canadians. There are several ways of doing things for people. We can intervene artificially- and I would say this was more or less the approach taken by the government of Ontario-by borrowing and passing the bill on to our children, meanwhile giving the impression that we did something. The important thing is to provide a climate in which Canadians can take care of their own development under the best possible conditions.
That is what we have done since 1984, and we were very successful if you consider the 1.5 million jobs that were created. After this recession we intend to let Canada launch its recovery on a solid basis.

Madam Speaker, there are often victims of bankruptcy who do not appear even in these numbers; those are the workers in these companies.
Other countries have political disappearances, we have economic disappearances. For instance, Brant Castings in Windsor went bankrupt a year ago and 100 workers have still not received any severance pay. The company failed to pay its pension contributions and half the workers are still unemployed.
What does this government have to say to Russ Jackson, Jim Leblanc and the other workers of Brant Castings? Why is there not a bankruptcy law reform in front of this House as was promised by the minister responsible many months ago?
May 24, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to tell the hon. member that he has a very good question about the bankruptcy law. I can tell him that he will soon have news from my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
The hon. member says that our policies are causing economic disappearance. I have views from people here who are business people and manufacturing people. They say that the NDP is killing factories and that their policies add to business costs. There is no easy way out of a recession. You can buy your way out once.
I would like to remind the House that when we came in, the government was spending $1.33 for every dollar it was bringing in. This makes people happy for a little while, but eventually it catches up with us. It has now, and we are getting Canada out of this mess.
Madam Speaker, such hypocrisy from a government which spends 34 cents of every dollar which it receives-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member will want to put his question. There have been long preambles to both previous questions.

Let me repeat for the Speaker the key point I want to put across.
The yearly Carleton University study, How Canada Spends, is coming out this week. It concludes that this government has no positive economic strategy.
I want to ask the minister if he will recognize that these growing bankruptcies call for a change in strategy. Will he recognize that he cannot talk about economic recovery in the face of these kinds of bankruptcies taking place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Whenever one particular manufacturer closes it is always very sad and it has, in some instances, a very dramatic impact, and I recognize that.
The hon. gentlemen, like most members from his party, thinks that he has a monopoly on caring. I can tell him that coming from a family of 21 children-and I am the 18th of the 21 children-from northwestern Quebec, bom in 1929, raised during the depression, I do not need lessons from him.
Oral Questions
There are right ways of solving problems and there are wrong ways. His way has been tried in eastern Europe and it has proven a failure.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
During the Iraq war, the Prime Minister condemned the international arms trade which helped Saddam Hussein build his aggressive military force and said Canada would not take part in this trade.
On February 20 the former Secretary of State said, and I quote: "It is imperative that the world declare that there be no Middle East arms bazaar; 95 per cent of the weapons in the hands of Saddam Hussein came from the five permanent members of the Security Council".
In light of these statements, how does the government justify Bill C-6?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-6 is designed to tighten up the restrictions on export of arms. We are providing for transparency. There will be a report to this Parliament on all the exports of arms made. There will be consultation with countries to which we propose to make arms sales. There will also be a need for Canada to have an arrangement with countries with which we have arms sales.
I want to stress to my hon. friend that what Bill C-6 does is provide additional controls on the sale of automatic weapons in excess of the existing controls that are there for higher powered weapons. So we are increasing the controls, not decreasing the controls.

Madam Speaker, for many years it has been Canada's policy not to sell arms to areas of conflict. The Middle East has had 26 wars since 1945, more than any other region, and except for Egypt there are no peace agreements between Israel and the Arab countries.
Why then is the government facilitating sales to this region? Who will be on the list of eligible countries for arms sales under the bill, and what controls will there be to prevent another aggression, such as we saw last summer?

May 24, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under this legislation each export permit will be decided on a case-by-case basis. There will be decisions taken that will judge whether the export will destabilize the region. If there has been an excessive buildup in arms in the region that will be taken into account in any decision as to whether or not a permit should be provided. I repeat, there will have to be an intergovernmental arrangement on defence, research and development production of any use of arms. That is the protection that we are providing to Canadians.
I would stress to my hon. friend that there will be additional controls on the export of automatic weapons as provided for under this Bill C-6 legislation. There will be additional controls over and above what is now provided for other exports of arms. This is a tightening up and an additional set of controls over and above what we have today.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the acting minister responsible for small business.
The government's high interest rate policy, its increased unemployment insurance premiums, its GST, have all diminished the ability of small business to lead the badly needed economic recovery in Canada and get us out of this recession.
I want to ask the minister when this government will provide relief to small business from the damage inflicted by this government's policies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
In the last eleven and a half months there has been a drop of about five percentage points in interest rates and that translates directly into relief for small businesses. I would say that is probably the greatest area of relief that we can provide.
I also point out to my hon. friend that there are many small businesses that are involved in the construction industry and, if she noticed, in the month of April there was a significant increase in housing starts. That is
supported by the drop in interest rates. It is also supported by the increase in the number of housing sales which is a reinforcement to the increase in housing starts.
One final point: My hon. friend mentioned the goods and services tax. We agree that the goods and services tax, when it is applied alongside the provincial sales tax, is an extra burden. We are working with the provinces and we encourage the provinces to harmonize their provincial sales taxes with the goods and services tax and in that way make a major contribution to lessening the burden of taxation on small businesses.

My supplementary is for the same minister.
Is the minister not aware that retail sales declined 3 per cent in the first four months of this year? That is the largest decline since the Diefenbaker government. It is the biggest drop in 30 years.
If the minister believes that this is grounds for optimism, that his government's policies are working, then this minister is badly out of touch with the needs of small business.
Will the minister admit that his government's policies have harmed the small business sector of this country and thus put at risk our ability to recover quickly from this recession?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology

We are in a period of recession. We are slowly coming out of it, and I suppose that that industry feels the pain.

Is the government aware of this and if it is, what is it going to do about it? If it is not aware of it, will it please look into it and do something about the effect of deregulation, something we predicted a long time ago.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
I wrote to the minister of employment last week and, indeed, I sent a notice today of my question regarding the severe ice conditions that currently prevail around the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, specifically the northeast coast and the northwest coast of the province.
The minister knows that fishermen's benefits ceased on May 15, that fishermen and their families have had no incomes since that time, and he knows that because of the severe ice conditions fishermen and their families have no means now of acquiring an income.
I want to ask the minister of employment who, indeed, as a former minister of fisheries, is aware of the severity of this problem, whether or not the government is going to extend unemployment insurance benefits for people who, through no fault of their own, have no income at this time of the year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can inform the hon. member and the House that my colleague, the minister of fisheries, and I are monitoring the situation closely. We are surveying these ice conditions on a daily basis along the west coast and the northeast coast of New-foundland-Labrador, and we will establish how ice conditions may be preventing fishermen from starting their regular season. We know that they have not started yet, as the member rightly points out.
The member also knows full well that this government has not hesitated in the past to meet and to assist the fishermen who are affected by severe ice conditions. We are monitoring the situation and we will respond accordingly.
May 24, 1991

Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer. Unfortunately, in past years, and this is not to look for an argument, the monitoring process has sometimes gone on so long that the suffering that results from a lack of income has been severe.
What fishermen and their families want, and I hope what the minister will give the House and through the House, fishermen and their families today, is an assurance of quick action. If it becomes clear, as it appears to be the case, that these are the worst ice conditions in some regions since 1974, that the minister will, as he is able to do, move quickly to restore those unemployment insurance benefits.
We are simply talking here of a case of fishermen and their families needing the dollars to prepare for the spring season to gear up for the fishery and, indeed, to keep their families and their children in clothing with bread and butter on the table.
Will the minister give us an assurance of quick action? We would appreciate that if he could.

We are standing ready. The last payments were May 15. They go for two weeks. We are monitoring the situation and hopefully will be able to act as quickly as possible.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Conservative member for North York, in her question, suggested that the taxpayers of her municipality, her constituency, the taxpayers of Ontario, were subsidizing western Canadians for RCMP services in western Canada.
The hon. member, in putting her question, is reflecting her total misunderstanding of the issue. It does not appear that the member knows anything at all about the role of the RCMP in western Canada. In fact, the provincial governments in western Canada are now
May 24, 1991

Supply
paying 70 per cent of the cost of providing RCMP services there under a contract that expired at the beginning of April.
As I indicated in my submissions, the Government of Canada is bent on destroying the RCMP in western Canada and, in fact, in Atlantic Canada and in the north. The RCMP is an important and essential national institution and the Conservative member for North York, speaking on behalf of the government, is saying to the people of western Canada, Atlantic Canada and the north that the federal government wants to get out of the business of providing RCMP services.
As I indicated in my comments, yesterday was the 118th birthday of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It was founded in 1873 as the North-West Mounted Police and it is a shame, a tragedy, that this government is now bent on destroying the RCMP by withdrawing its fair share of funding. The RCMP provides an essential service to communities in the western Canadian provinces.
If the RCMP were withdrawn, it would be a serious blow to national unity. As I indicated earlier, the RCMP is a highly respected police force. It is one of the finest police forces anywhere in the world. Indeed, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is recognized world-wide for its thoroughness and its efficiency. Indeed, the motto of the RCMP is that it always gets its person.
On behalf of the Official Opposition, we would like to send a very definite and clear message to the Solicitor General who is here in the House today. That message is to negotiate in good faith. The provinces that contract for RCMP services, the provinces that do not have their own provincial police forces, are not asking for anything more. All they are asking is that the federal government negotiate in good faith to continue paying its share, that is 30 per cent of police services in western Canada and in Atlantic Canada. They want to continue the contract that expired on April 1. They believe it was a good contract.
Unfortunately, the government has not been acting in good faith. Hopefully, as a result of the debate here today, the Solicitor General, who I note is listening very attentively, will instruct his officials immediately to consummate and negotiate a new contract on the basis of fairness and equity.
