subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend's motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take into full account the budgetary reality of the provinces and municipalities involved in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police contract negotiations and therefore be prepared to negotiate a contract for RCMP services which does not unfairly transfer policing costs from the federal government to provincial and municipal governments.
This motion could not have been presented at a more opportune time. I was appointed Solicitor General just over a month ago. I have had an opportunity to brief myself on the RCMP contract file. I took the occasion to fly to Vancouver and meet with my colleagues, the solicitor general of British Columbia and the attorney General of Manitoba. In fact, I discussed this file with the solicitor general of British Columbia as recently as this week. The file is very current.
In the short time that I have been the Solicitor General, I have also had an opportunity to discuss this file with my cabinet colleagues, particularly those who serve as members of the Treasury Board.
I met the Treasury Board ministers concerning this issue at nine o'clock this morning.
I am grateful to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni for the timeliness of his motion and the way in which it is worded. The motion is not derogatory, it is not inflammatory, and it allows us to have a fair and frank exposure of the issue without a great deal of political posturing.
I am also very grateful for the opportunity that this motion presents me, as the Solicitor General of Canada and as the minister responsible for the RCMP contract negotiations, to share with the House and with the public the federal government's position in these negotiations.
At the outset there should be an appreciation of the scale of the contract policing program. There are approximately 10,000 RCMP officers, almost one-half of the entire force, engaged in contract policing. The RCMP are providing the policing services under contract to all provinces, except Ontario and Quebec, and to the two territories and some 191 municipalities within the provinces and territories. The federal government shares the cost of providing RCMP policing services with the provinces, territories, and municipalities that use the RCMP, on terms that were last negotiated in 1981.
It is also important at the outset that there be an appreciation that the federal government remains committed to the RCMP and the RCMP policing program. There has been no suggestion in these negotiations that it has been any part of the federal government's agenda to remove the RCMP from its contract policing responsibilities. Notwithstanding the expiration of the present contract on March 31, 1991, the RCMP has remained on site and remained on duty providing the same high level of policing duties after March 31 that it was providing before March 31, 1991.
As all members of the House will know, the 1981 agreements expired on March 31,1991. The negotiations for a new contract have been stalled for some time as a result of a disagreement over the allocation of costs, particularly over the question of the proposed increase from 70 to 75 per cent of the provincial share of the cost of provincial policing services.
The federal government has been seeking in these negotiations to achieve a more appropriate apportionment of the costs of provincial, territorial and municipal policing. For their part the contract jurisdictions have acknowledged, without specifically committing themselves, that the cost base should be adjusted to ensure that it more fairly and fully reflects the costs of delivering RCMP policing service to the provinces, the territories, and the municipalities that are receiving that service.
May 24, 1991

I want to digress for just a minute, if I may, to emphasize that we are not talking about the costs associated with the federal law enforcement responsibilities of the RCMP. In addition to its contract responsibilities, the RCMP also has significant federal law enforcement responsibilities. I am referring here to the RCMP's responsibilities for the enforcement of federal legislation relating to drugs, customs, immigration and the like, as well as to its responsibilities for protective policing and the enforcement of executive orders.
Those responsibilities are exclusively federal responsibilities and the costs associated with those responsibilities are therefore borne exclusively by the federal government. The costs of federal law enforcement therefore are not an issue in these negotiations.
What is at issue in these negotiations is the share of the provincial, territorial and municipal policing costs that should be borne by the contract jurisdictions. The provinces, and this is fair, are questioning the federal government's proposal that a more appropriate sharing of the costs would be 75 per cent provincial, 25 per cent federal. Their suggestion is that the 1981 agreement was definitive and permanent in establishing a 70-30 split of costs.
I want to make two points that I think are relevant to that. First of all, I would point out to the House that the provincial share of costs has been moving up over the years as the provinces grew in size and became more capable of paying for the service.
The provincial share in 1928 was 40 per cent. In 1971 it was increased to 56 per cent, and between 1981 and 1991 the provincial share went from 56 per cent to 70 per cent.
I imagine that the 70-30 compromise was taken with the realization that the increase was substantial and therefore should be tempered.
However, the historical trend is clear. I think it is really a question of the provinces assuming a greater portion of their financial responsibility consistent with their constitutional responsibility for the administration of justice, including provincial and municipal policing.
Supply
Second, by contrast with the 1981 agreements, I think it is fair to say the present federal offer is a very modest one. Apart from some adjustments to the base to ensure that the costs of delivering the service are more fairly reflected, we are only asking that the provinces pay an additional 5 per cent of the costs of RCMP provincial policing, an increase that we are prepared to phase in over time.
What we have here, then, is a gradual movement toward a more accurate matching of costs and benefits. In fact, we believe that we are suggesting a fairer rather than an unfair treatment of policing costs.
We acknowledge that there is a federal benefit in RCMP contract policing. It has been suggested that the 1985 Neilsen report established the federal benefit at 30 per cent.
I understand that the 1985 Neilsen report concluded that it was impossible to quantify the federal benefit with any precision. It went on to suggest that the real provincial and municipal burdens were lighter than the cost share ratios would indicate since the cost base only partly reflected the cost of delivering the service.
I suggest that the cost share ratios established in 1981 represented an incremental assumption by the contract provinces of a greater measure of their financial responsibility consistent, as I say once again, with their constitutional responsibility for the administration of justice, including provincial and municipal policing.
It would be consistent with the entire history of the RCMP contract policing which has been characterized by graduated increases in the provincial shares of the costs of the policing service.
It also has to be appreciated that over the last 10 years the cost share ratios have been applied to a negotiated cost base. For example, for some reason the cost base excludes the employer's contribution to unemployment insurance premiums. The Auditor General of Canada has noted this anomaly several times, specifically in his audit of Saskatchewan, and said that that should be included.
Second, only a portion of the employer's contribution to RCMP pensions is included in the cost base.

May 24, 1991
Supply
Third, concerning accommodation charges, when the federal government rents to the provinces it is one-third of comparable market rates. We find that when the provinces rent to us, however, we are paying market rates. There has to be an adjustment there.
In my preliminary discussions with Ivan Messmer of British Columbia and Jim McCrae of Manitoba, I sensed that there was a willingness to reach a fair cost base structure, and I am sure we can make progress on that particular issue.
What is at issue is the value to the provinces and contracting municipalities that they receive from contract policing. Speaking as a chartered accountant, I would suggest that this is not quantifiable in terms of dollars and cents as we can quantify some of the things in the cost base.
I think one has to look at what it would cost the province or municipality if it were doing it on its own. Rather than pontificating on this from a lofty federal viewpoint, I want to refer the House to an opinion recently expressed by Dennis Moffatt, an alderman from Red Deer, Alberta, the same municipality which was referred to by my hon. friend opposite in his remarks. This exchange took place on Alberta News Hour on April 26, 1991.
The reporter says:
Dennis Moffatt sat on the local council for 15 years and has heard the complaint before, that the RCMP are too expensive. He says: "Even if the city has to pay 100 per cent of the bill, it is still a good buy".

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
When we buy a constable, he comes equipped with uniform, training out of Regina and Ottawa, a car, radio back-up, access to laboratories right across the country, access to Interpol, the FBI, the CIA, the MI-5 right across the board. We would have to pay for that at the municipalities if we did it by ourselves.
What Mr. Moffatt was talking about were the benefits of the economies of scale that the provinces and the municipalities receive from the RCMP contract policing. Duplication is eliminated in areas such as communications, computer systems, management structure, recruiting, training, personnel services and in a number of operational support areas, including fingerprint identification services, dog services and air and marine services.
When I was in B.C. I had occasion to discuss this matter with some officers out there. It occurred to me as
a layman that there are some benefits I have not mentioned.
If the RCMP has a constable who has reached his or her level of excellence in one province and is looking for a greater challenge, an opportunity to further his or her career and if there is a need in a larger province or another opportunity for that particular individual, then there is so much more flexibility in the RCMP and the provinces, be they large or small, to get a better constable. That is another benefit which I would say accrues to the provinces.
It may be difficult to assign dollar values to these benefits, but I believe they represent significant benefits to the contract provinces and the territories.
I mention these benefits because I am concerned that they are not always given the prominence I think they deserve.
In addition to the direct benefits that I have described above, there are also a number of significant indirect and intangible benefits which are enjoyed by the provinces, the territories and the municipalities that contract for RCMP policing services. Some of these are as follows.
First, law enforcement services: These include the Canadian Police Information Centre, a large computer centre that police can use via terminals to check on stolen vehicles, criminal records and missing persons, the Canadian Police College and the forensic lab. These services are available to the entire Canadian police community at no charge. Again it is the federal government that covers these costs.
Second, non-police duties: The RCMP, particularly in remote regions, performs a number of duties that are strictly speaking not police duties. I am talking about issuing lottery licences, inspecting vehicles on behalf of the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, et cetera. There have been some recent RCMP estimates that the RCMP dedicates as much as 30 person-years to serving as prosecutors on behalf of the Attorney General of Newfoundland. It is the federal government that covers these costs on behalf of the provinces and the territories.
Third, the Corps of Commissionaires at division and subdivision levels: Although the facilities at the division and subdivision levels are often being used by three levels of government, all security costs are charged to the federal government.
May 24, 1991

Fourth, divisional staff relations representatives program and labour challenges through the Federal Court: All of the labour related costs of the RCMP, from association to litigation, are carried by the federal government. The contract jurisdictions are receiving their policing free of the labour related charges. Put more directly, the contract divisions are receiving a strike free policing service and again the federal government covers the cost of this benefit.
Five, civil actions, compensation claims and ex gratia payments: The contract jurisdictions are receiving their policing free of all the legal liabilities that ordinarily are attached to a police force. The federal government pays 100 per cent of these costs.
Six, centralized audit and program evaluation: There are a number of smaller items, which are impossible to quantify with any precision, which come into this. I am speaking of centralized audit programs, bulk buying, et cetera. The federal government carries the entire burden of these costs.
Most important perhaps, the federal government makes a considerable contribution over and above the contracts to building and maintaining high national policing standards and the contract jurisdictions get the benefit of that contribution at no additional cost.
In the short time that I have had the privilege to serve as Solicitor General I have developed a very real concern that perhaps the contract jurisdictions do not fully appreciate the cost advantages of the RCMP on the street, as it were. As a recent report of the British Columbia police services branch acknowledged, the RCMP provides what is probably the most frugal policing service in the country.
This conclusion is borne out by data produced by the Canadian Centre for Justice Statistics, a division of Statistics Canada. These data tell us that on a per capita basis, that is per capita of provincial residents, each resident of Ontario is paying $245.14 for the provincial policing service. Similarly, each resident of Quebec is paying $247.04 for the provincial policing service.
Supply
By contrast, each resident of British Columbia is paying $136.26 for the provincial policing service. That is quite a saving compared to Ontario and Quebec. In Nova Scotia each provincial resident is paying only $80.68 for the RCMP provincial policing service.
Put another way, using Ontario and Quebec as reference points, policing services would cost the contract provinces on average more than twice as much as they are now paying if they were to establish their own police forces. The cost sharing formula in the RCMP contract policing is in need of review in order that-to paraphrase the words of my hon. colleague, the member for Com-ox-Albemi-the policing costs fairly reflect the RCMP services which the provinces and the municipalities receive.
In conclusion I say we, the federal government, seek a fair apportionment of the policing costs in the provinces and the municipalities in which the RCMP provides services. We are conscious of their fiscal realities. We are sure that they are conscious of ours.
We are both conscious of the fact that the RCMP, through its national service, serves as an effective national operation which benefits federal, provincial and municipal jurisdictions.
We do not seek to put at risk this national institution because of a need to budget. Effectiveness and essentials can often transcend dollars and cents. That is what we seek to do. I am confident that we can do it.

that unify this country, we are looking at the RCMP as most definitely one of those.
I have come here to not only praise the RCMP but also to criticize it as a Quebecer. No matter which contract is agreed upon with the provinces, I would like to request a response from the Solicitor General that his attention be paid to the most recent tendency of politicians to put their cotton picking hands into the RCMP's business.
As a Quebecer I can speak to you about barn burning, I can speak to you about raids on political parties' membership lists and, most recently, I can speak to you from my own riding about a former member of Parliament. While he was under investigation the search warrant being carried out was delayed deliberately. It was a political decision because that former member of Parliament was a candidate in that election. I was a candidate at the same time in the same riding. Only after that member of Parliament won was a search warrant carried out.
What happens to the RCMP is that when we get it politically involved, it loses its fine reputation temporarily, but it takes a chink out of the armour. I would request that the gentleman on the other side, the Solicitor General, be veiy, very careful that does not occur again.
There is just one more recent case which has always been bothering me since I have been here in this House. It deals with a political decision with the RCMP on bilingual bonuses. Bilingual bonuses are approximately in the amount of $800. They were supposed to be paid since 1976 to RCMP members. They have not been paid. There was a judgment of the Federal Court of Canada in March, 1990, which said that the $800 bilingual bonuses should be paid. In the same judgment, Gingras v. Her Majesty the Queen, Judge Dube said: "The question, therefore, is whether the board enjoys a discretion"-I am talking about the Treasury Board which has refused to pay these bilingual bonuses-"and it can, with impunity, ignore its own policies and impose an unofficial exclusion which was never stated in the policy". In other words, the Treasury Board abused its powers and therefore acted illegally.
Judge Dube said that the Treasury Board acted illegally and abused its powers.
I have a paper here from the RCMP Association. RCMP members are not allowed to have a union as such.
They have a French and English association. They were talking about this court case as a possibility where they could obtain a bonus which was legitimately theirs since 1976, a bonus which generally reaffirms our commitment to two official languages. At the time of the writing of this internal document from the RCMP Association, there was great hope that they would be able to get the bilingual bonus because the case had just been won.
There was a political decision to be made. Do we appeal this decision or do we give these RCMP members their money?
According to this document, and I just want to quote it briefly and then I will listen to the Solicitor General's response, the members of the RCMP say:

"According to the uncontradicted testimony of Mr. Gaston Guenette, an official language policy officer at the Treasury Board Secretariat, no ministerial order has excluded non-civilian members of the RCMP from the bonus. The decision came from Cabinet and was communicated to the RCMP by the Board. The Board's decision was influenced by the opinions, fears and pressures of the RCMP Commissioner. Given Mr. Guenette's testimony, there is reason to fear that the Commissioner was certainly involved in the decision in question."
Finally, they add that this matter was brought up with one of the predecessors of the Solicitor General, the Hon. Pierre Blais, and they mentioned that he was in agreement that this bilingual bonus be paid and he was bringing that before Treasuiy Board.

It is becoming a language issue between English and French and it is not conducive to the proper, efficient functioning of the RCMP. I would like to ask the minister if he would look into this, as he has looked into other things which I have presented and has done a very good job, and get back to me on the possibility of doing something about this sore which is festering between English and French speaking officers in the RCMP.

Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of debate today.
It is very useful that there is an opportunity to debate the question of policing and the cost of policing in Canada. I am pleased that the Solicitor General, the minister responsible for the RCMP, is in the House to hear the concerns of members of the House.
The cost of policing and the level of policing is an extremely important issue today. The level of policing in the community of Campbell River, British Columbia has created concerns that more police officers are required. It is like many other communities.
We have a recession going on. During the recession crime has continued to rise pretty dramatically. The crime that is happening is unusual. There is the standard form of break and enter in which a professional individual breaks into an establishment.
It is hard to tell that the individual has entered. The most valuable material is removed. There is very little damage, and indeed, there is very little indication of the entry and theft.
Then there is the other kind of situation, of which there is apparently an enormous increase in communities, in which an individual breaks into a home, restaurant, or another operation and removes things like cigarettes, food, and small amounts of money. It is almost subsistence stealing. This is occurring during a period of recession and high unemployment.
The kind of action that will deter that type of activity is more attention by government to support of social services and, as well, more policing. This is absolutely not the time to create a situation where we are going to see a reduction in policing.
An increase of 27 to 30 per cent in the operating budget of a small community because of increased policing costs is certainly going to be a deterrent to any expansion in policing. Indeed, we are going to see cuts in policing.
At a time when crime is rising in many areas this is absolutely critical. This must be put on the back burner. The minister and the government should begin to negotiate and be willing to go to the table with the provinces involved and make some accommodation during this very difficult time.

May 24, 1991
Supply
In one area that I represent on the Sechelt peninsula there are two communities, the town of Gibsons and the district of Sechelt. They recently underwent an enormous expansion of population which is growing very rapidly. Unfortunately, there has been no expansion in police services in that community.
The other thing that happened in that community was a major expansion to the pulp mill. In my recollection, the pulp mill took on about 1,600 people, mainly single men who arrived in the community to work on the mill construction. They lived in bunk houses creating considerable stress in the community.
In addition, we had at one point 200 pipeline workers from the province of Alberta who arrived on the Sechelt peninsula to put in a gas pipeline. They were there for a few months, and then they were gone. Again, that created enormous stress.
On many occasions, there was a single police officer to deal with the entire area. Something on the order of
1.800	single men, or men who were by themselves, in the community created a substantial strain.
In one altercation in the emergency ward of the St. Mary's Hospital a nurse was unable to get police assistance. There just was not a police officer to be had. They wound up having to phone Vancouver to see if they could dispatch somebody.
News of the concern eventually reached my office and the local RCMP and the RCMP said: "Look, we are using all the people we have to the maximum extent they can be used". Ultimately the conclusions of the municipalities, the regional board, and everyone on that peninsula is that they needed more policing and that no consideration was being given to the natural growth of a community which is a bedroom community of Vancouver and is growing extremely rapidly.
There was no consideration given to the quick 1,600 or
1.800	increase in the population because of the pipeline and mill constructions. That cannot be allowed to continue in an area as it could create a very unsafe situation for people.
It is incumbent upon the Solicitor General and the Government of Canada to ensure they do not make these cuts in funding at this time and cut policing in the municipalities even further. The federal government has a responsibility to assist the provinces in providing adequate levels of policing in those communities and in determining how to solve those problems, rather than to create problems and make them more intense.
In the community of Sechelt there has been talk of hiring private police. Break and entry of businesses is rising at a rapid rate and business people in the community are now taking a look at how they might hire people to take on police and security work. There is talk of vigilantes. This, of course, is absolutely not an acceptable direction to go.
It is ironic that the scepticism expressed by many of the people is that this is what the federal government wants. It wants privatization of services. This is the direction it will move in. So the people will hire their own police force. That is the direction they see. There is a lack of care and concern on the part of the federal government.
I would suspect that there are groups meeting. There have been discussions in Campbell River on Vancouver Island. This is going to happen. There are very serious concerns about the number of break-ins of homes and businesses and the people are very, very concerned about the level of policing.
There are discussions now on how people in the business community and the core of the community can create their own private operations to try and give them a little more security and a little more safety. This has to happen.
The federal government has to fight the increase of police forces in the hands of a number of individuals and look at providing better levels of trained, professional peace officers in those communities. This is moving in a very dangerous direction. I see a population out there that is very sceptical about this government's concern for their well-being.
The costs that are going to fall on small communities of 5,000 or more people are enormous. Their operating budgets have been hammered very badly.
I would like to use the example of the community of Alert Bay on northern Vancouver Island. Alert Bay has had an interesting encounter with this federal government. It has a Coast Guard radio station which provides about 13 jobs for this very small community of about
1,000	and a native community of about 900 people. The Conservative government decided that it was time to remove those 13 jobs from a community that can ill afford to lose them. They were terminated in spite of some very constructive cost-saving proposals which were totally ignored. The government has now adopted the Prime Minister's slogan: "I do not care how unpopular it is. I know best". So it did not listen to Alert Bay. It did not listen to northern Vancouver Island and the people's suggestions on how it could be made more efficient and how some of the economic benefits could be retained. Out it went.
May 24, 1991

Seven federal government jobs in the RCMP marine division were moved out of Alert Bay. They are gone. Again the Prime Minister knows best and the community is damaged.
There are cuts to the postal service, and the Prime Minister knows best.
Johnstone Strait communities are based on fishing. It was decided to drastically cut the Johnstone Strait fisheries. This fishery is absolutely critical to Alert Bay. It provides seasonal jobs for the Indian community and the non-Indian community. No, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans knows best. It is going to cut down on fishing in Johnstone Strait and limit the ability of these people to earn an income.
They are up in arms over this. Ottawa does not care. It does not care about the jobs provided by the RCMP marine division. It does not care about the Coast Guard radio station. It does not care about the hundreds and hundreds of jobs related to the Johnstone Strait fisheries. It is going to get rid of them.
To add insult to injury it was decided to make it harder to get unemployment insurance. Now, these people cannot get work. They want to work in traditional jobs as they have always done but they cannot do it. They hope they can feed their families by qualifying for more than 10 weeks of unemployment insurance. But no, fisheries and oceans and the Government of Canada will not do it. Many of those people are now collecting welfare because of this federal government.
Another insult added to injury is that fisheries and oceans-again the Conservative government knows best-decided it was going to eliminate Alert Bay as a port of landing for halibut, for sable fish. Even though there are two producers in that community, they are gone.
Turning to policing costs, Alert Bay will get less policing out of the northern Vancouver Island thing because of what is going on with the federal government today. In the middle of a recession the community is being devastated by this government. Policing services,
Supply
which are desperately needed there, are going to be cut back as well.
It is ironic that this is being done at a time when the Prime Minister of Canada is asking the people of Alert Bay to become concerned about national unity, to become concerned about all of us as Canadians with the federal government as a focal point. Those people are saying: "The best thing I can expect from the federal government is another poke in the eye with a sharp stick."
When we talk about national unity, there are still some very strong Canadians there who totally blame the Prime Minister and the government for the misfortune that has befallen them. Every individual, every business, every person in the fishing industry in that community cannot wait to vote against the government.
Just a stone's throw across the water from Alert Bay is the community of Port Hardy. Port Hardy has suffered under the lash of this uncaring government. Port Hardy is a community of close to 5,000 people. It was a growing, healthy and a vibrant place to be and in the 1981 census it went over 5,000. As a result of having a population over
5,000,	they wound up having to pay policing costs which were a substantial part of their operating budget. All of a sudden, the recession came on the next year, in 1982, and their population base collapsed. It went down to 4,000. I listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member and would like to comment.
Port Hardy is familiar to me because my daughter and son-in-law worked as physicians there, and I can confirm what he is saying. They said this community was devastated by the policies of this government. So I perfectly agree with what he was saying.
I would like to point out as well that the principle of the contract we are negotiating with the eight provinces and two territories was established in 1981. One of the principles was that 70 per cent of the services provided by the RCMP in those provinces and territories were under the Criminal Code and provincial statutes. This is why the provinces agreed to pay 70 per cent of the costs. Thirty per cent of the services were federal statutes and laws like immigration, drug enforcement, migratory birds, wildlife, and white collar crime.
Therefore, a principle was established that 30 per cent of the activities of the RCMP in a given province were of federal jurisdiction. Now the Solicitor General tells them: "We want to pay only 25 per cent, and you pay 75 per cent". Naturally, you are shifting the burden on the taxpayer of that province.
As far as the municipalities are concerned, they were paying 90 per cent for the services of the RCMP and the federal government only 10 per cent. This was logical; they accepted that.
Therefore, I think what the government does is put the burden on the taxpayers of that province. I listened before to another member here, I think she was a Conservative, who said: "But you know, Quebec and Ontario are subsidizing the RCMP to do the policing duties in the other provinces". I think one thing they forget is that the RCMP performs duties in the province of Quebec and Ontario. There are about 2,000 officers in those provinces that are being paid by the federal government. Quebec and Ontario do not contribute a cent to those services. Therefore it is a false argument.
Another principle that was established is that if you have a national police force like the RCMP it is an efficiency factor. It is better to have one police force than to have three or four. The cost is lower. This is what is happening in those provinces where the RCMP provides services. So it is extremely important that you maintain efficiency and cut the costs, and one of the ways of cutting costs is by having a national police force.

May 24, 1991

The third principle that was established in 1981 when those negotiations were taking place is that the RCMP was a symbol of national unity. This government talks continuously about national unity, of the symbolism of our institutions, but it is trying to destroy the most important symbol of Canada that everybody around the world knows, namely, the RCMP. Canadians all over the world are known as having a national police force that is extremely efficient.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it significant that the motion before this House today should encourage the government to conclude contract policing agreements which do not "unfairly transfer policing costs" to the contracting jurisdictions. The motion is, in my view, an indication of the general lack of understanding and appreciation which exists within the NDP for the size and importance of the role of the RCMP in providing federal, protective policing and law enforcement services to all Canadians.
In view of the present circumstances surrounding the ongoing contract negotiations, it is understandable that much of the public's attention has been focused on the contract policing role of the RCMP. While contract policing is a major part of the RCMP's function, it should be emphasized that a large percentage of RCMP personnel and resources are engaged in non-contract activities paid for in their entirety by the federal government. You would never know that after listening to the NDP here today.
These activities such as federal law enforcement, protective policing, and law enforcement services, provide substantial benefits to communities across Canada regardless of whether or not they are served by RCMP contract policing detachments.
It is important that during these ongoing federal-provincial negotiations for renewal of the policing contracts the parties directly involved and, indeed, all Canadians should remind themselves of the important services provided by the RCMP to all levels of government and to all citizens.
When considering the motion which is before the House it is important that hon. members be fully informed of the extent to which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police provides law enforcement and police services to all Canadians and of the extent to which those services are provided without cost to the provinces and municipalities.
Supply
Most Canadians, especially those outside Ontario and Quebec, are aware that the RCMP provides contract policing to a number of provincial and territorial jurisdictions. This fact is perhaps one of the most evident aspects of RCMP activities because it is probably the force's most visible program. The presence of the Mounties in eight of the 10 provinces, the two territories, and close to 200 municipalities in a contract policing role is as visible and apparent as that of city or provincial police in Ontario and Quebec. Citizens recognize the force and rightly so as a symbol of trust, authority, law and order. Members from both political parties referred to the RCMP as one of the best police forces in the world. I wish they could give me their list of who they think is better or who tops this list if the RCMP is only one of the best.
Notwithstanding the importance of this role, the RCMP performs a number of other vital functions to ensure the safety and security of all Canadians.
Members will appreciate that the RCMP maintains a federal policing complement in each of the 10 provinces and two territories. The RCMP federal policing complements attend to such federal responsibilities as policing at international and domestic airports, commercial crime investigations, protective policing of visiting dignitaries and other VIPs, as well as providing support to customs operations and drug law enforcement, something that is of particular importance coming as I do from the Niagara peninsula which is a border area.
Since federal policing units are dedicated solely to the enforcement of federal legislation and executive orders, the costs associated with these activities are paid for entirely by the federal government. You may have missed that if you followed, as I am sure you have, Madam Speaker, the debate here this morning. You would not be able to guess by listening to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that these services are paid for in total by the federal government-

In addition to its specific federal law enforcement function, the RCMP provides law enforcement support services to all Canadian law enforcement agencies.

May 24, 1991
Supply
These services provide technical and operational support to provincial and municipal police forces and ensure that the latest police technology and techniques are available to provincial and municipal police forces across Canada.
Law enforcement services are provided to local police forces regardless of their size or ability to pay and help to assist in maintaining a high national standard of criminal investigations. These services are funded by the federal government in the interest of maintaining the safety and security of all Canadians.
The combination of federal law enforcement activities and the provision of law enforcement services to Canadian police forces constitutes an important part of RCMP program activities. They are important not only to the federal government and to the RCMP but of course to the communities and local police forces that benefit from these services.
Federal expenditures on RCMP activities constitute a significant portion of RCMP resource levels. Indeed, revenues from all services rendered, including contract policing services, amount to only 30 per cent of the cost of the RCMP's law enforcement program.
For instance, in the 1988-89 fiscal year, the RCMP spent over $400 million on the enforcement of federal statutes and executive orders and over $125 million on the provision of law enforcement services. Expenditures on these program activities have increased in the last two years, to a combined total of $546 million in 1989-90 and $639 million in 1990-91. These combined activities thus represent program expenditures which are over three-quarters of the size of contract policing expenditures over the same period.
I would like to take this opportunity to give hon. members a wider appreciation of the variety and quality of services which are provided to Canadians by the RCMP and which are funded by the federal government. I do that, of course, because as I indicated earlier we might wait a long time before we hear the NDP mention some of these things.
I am confident that once this information is before the House, members' concerns about the transfer of policing costs from the federal government to provincial and municipal governments will be allayed.
The RCMP acts within its mandate to prevent, detect and investigate offences against federal statutes and to provide investigational assistance and security advice to other federal departments and agencies as required.
This responsibility involves the force's participation in the enforcement of over 40 major federal statutes from the Aeronautics Act to the Young Offenders Act. The force's Customs and Excise Program investigates smuggling and offences involving the illicit manufacturing of spirits or tobacco products, offences under the Excise Act. It is also responsible for investigating illegal trans-border shipping of strategic goods, high technology and cultural property.
The Mounties also enforce Canada's fight against the problem of illegal trafficking in endangered wildlife species. The Immigration and Passport Program assists in the enforcement of the Immigration and Citizenship Acts as well as the investigations of Canadian passport regulations under the Criminal Code.
Special Services provides support to investigators in technical and physical surveillance, polygraph examination, audio and video analysis and personality profiles of violent criminals. The force also maintains a special emergency response team which is trained to resolve terrorist hostage-taking incidents and related crises which may be beyond the normal capabilities of regular RCMP personnel and other police forces.
The War Crimes Investigation Unit works to bring to justice persons suspected of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Two areas of federal enforcement, drug enforcement and economic crimes, are areas of particular emphasis by the RCMP. The relatively large number of resources assigned to these initiatives reflects their priority for the federal government.
Currently, over 1,000 persons and approximately $84 million are committed to the investigation of offences relating to the importation, exportation, trafficking and possession of narcotics and other prohibited drugs in Canada. Federal drug sections co-operate with local police in drug enforcement activities and the operation of drug prevention and awareness programs.
May 24, 1991

The RCMP federal drug sections in connection with the contracting policing resources provide street level drug enforcement services across Canada.
Approximately 600 persons and $41 million are devoted to the specialized investigation of economic crime. This includes the investigation of fraudulent bankruptcies, violations of the Income Tax Act and the UI Act, counterfeiting, computer crime, and other forms of business-oriented crime.
In 1989, the economic crime program provided assistance in over 4,000 investigations which resulted in recoveries of almost $42 million by affected parties.
In addition to federal law enforcement, the RCMP is also responsible for discharging the government's protective policing obligations and providing security services to a range of federal properties, office-holders, and dignitaries.
Security services are provided to the Governor General, the Prime Minister and their families, as well as to foreign missions and visiting dignitaries. Federal properties such as Parliament Hill, Government House and the Supreme Court are also provided with security arrangements by the RCMP.
I am certain that in the course of most members' travels to and from their constituencies they have had occasion to see a member of the RCMP patrolling Canada's airports. Their uniformed presence at these facilities is the most visible part of the force's airport protective policing program which provides security services at 10 international and eight major domestic airports. Specially trained and armed personnel patrol critical access points inside terminals and aircraft operating areas to prevent and detect security incidents.
Resources devoted to the airport policing program in the current year total 895 person-years and approximately $75 million.
The RCMP maintains a small core of personnel which provides advice and expertise to ensure that security procedures at special events are in place to ensure the safety of participants. In this way the force contributes invaluable security advice and guidance to the planning of major events across Canada.
In 1990 the Royal Canadian Mounted Police co-ordinated 28 special events and was consulted on preparations for a further 52. Depending on annual
Supply
requirements these events can range from state visits to major economic summits and major sporting events such as the Winter Olympics held recently in Calgary.
Protective policing services are estimated to account for 12.8 per cent of total RCMP expenditures and 9.7 per cent of person-years for 1991-92.
The Law Enforcement Services Program provides specialized services to the RCMP as well as to other law enforcement agencies, corrections agencies, government departments, and criminal courts. These services support participating agencies in exercising their responsibilities for maintaining peace, order, and security.
The Canadian Police Information Centre provides and maintains an automated national information system for the storage, retrieval and exchange of operational police information on behalf of all accredited Canadian police agencies. This program, along with the management of information, resources, and services required to support other RCMP programs, will account for over 1,700 person-years and about $155 million in RCMP expenditures for the current fiscal year.
The $31 million Forensic Laboratory Service Program provides scientific and technical assistance for the benefit of the Canadian criminal justice system. The program provides analysis of physical evidence acquired during the course of investigations and expert opinions based on scientific examinations to aid investigations and for use as court evidence.
In addition to court and investigative assistance, forensic scientific support is provided to participating agencies in the areas of developmental and technical training. Consulting services and training assistance may also be provided to other government departments and foreign countries.
Roughly $59 million of the RCMP's current resource allocation is allocated to the provision of identification services. This program maintains a centralized criminal records function supported by fingerprints for use by police agencies and other aspects of the criminal justice system.
Identification Services provides photographic processing and printing services, maintains records of restricted firearms, and examines fraudulent cheques and hold-up notes for similarities with other documents on file.

May 24, 1991
Supply
This program is also responsible for maintaining the missing children's registry which holds records on children who have been reported missing across Canada. The registry shares information with other police agencies and the media to assist in locating these children.
The RCMP also operates the Canadian Police College program, which provides advanced police training in organizational and administrative personnel management and specialized investigative techniques to assist law enforcement agencies. The college operates on a budget of about $9 million and provides training to over
2,000	candidates annually.
Criminal Intelligence Services Canada is a national organization which is administered by the RCMP and which focuses on gathering and sharing information on organized crime and tactical intelligence. The service provides facilities for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of criminal intelligence and ensures that the relevant intelligence is submitted to provincial bureaus. In this way the flow of information between units provides all Canadian police agencies with access to organized crime intelligence.
As I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, I have attempted to provide a brief overview of the many and varied services which are provided by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the benefit of all Canadians.
In addition to the important and high profile contract policing services, the force devotes a sizeable portion of its resources to federal law enforcement, protective policing, and law enforcement services. In many cases these non-contract services provide considerable investigative and professional support, both directly and indirectly, to the contracting jurisdictions.
The government is pleased to reaffirm its continuing commitment and support for the RCMP's important national role in providing non-contract policing services, at federal expense, to all Canadian communities.

I wonder if, in calculating the costs, the additional costs of running the RCMP have been added to the mix and charged out to the provinces. If so, I submit that this is the part that is unfair. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary could address that particular question more directly.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by expanding the motion from my NDP colleague to include the jurisdiction of the two territories in addition to the provinces, with respect to the transfer of police costs.
The government of the Northwest Territories is currently paying for 70 per cent of the cost of the RCMP in the north. The federal government expects, unrealistically, that the territorial government can now absorb 75 per cent of the cost. That is a big jump in the proportion contributed by the territorial government.
There are extraordinary needs in the north that cannot be equated with southern needs. One such is the fact that there is a heavy reliance on the RCMP in the north to travel to various communities because members are not stationed in each of the communities in the north.
There is a heavy reliance on capital refurbishment because of the use of ski-doos and trucks which do not have the luxury of travelling on paved highways, but gravel roads and winter roads where they are available. There is also the use of Twin Otters, one of which, unfortunately, crashed in a community. There was much
debate as to whether that would be replaced. Much capital infrastructure is needed in the communities where they travel only by air and they do not have highways and roads.
The territorial government would rather invest its money in providing more and better service. For instance, the Yellowknife detachment of the RCMP is seriously understaffed. We have a high transient population and this is the feeder community for all of the outlying communities. We have a high incidence of people coming from out of town, a high transient population that needs to be served.
As well, there are communities that do not even have resident RCMP. Some communities in the Keewatin region are served only once a month. There are communities that should have full-time service and others that should have more frequent visits. The federal government cannot ignore the unique situation which the two territories present to the role of the RCMP.
The Yukon and Northwest Territories encompass an area of some 3.9 million square miles, covering 40 per cent of Canada, spanning more than 4,000 kilometres from west to east, and 3,500 kilometres from north to south. As I have said time and again in this House, the north is an immense region which is of strategic importance to all Canadians.
Let me explain what the challenges are in providing policing service in an area of this size. Although two-thirds of the Yukon's 25,800 live in and around Whitehorse, less than one-quarter of the Northwest Territories' population of 54,000 live in Yellowknife. The rest live in some 100 smaller communities scattered across the north. The federal government, rather than expecting the territorial governments to put up more money to cover the cost of policing, should be looking at how the north can receive support for better policing services for those residents living in northern communities.
As well, the government should be investing in methods for the RCMP to take steps to strengthen its relationship with the aboriginal people who are the majority in the north, as well as the other people who live in the remote regions. The government has to continue to develop community policing concepts and special recruitment drives for attracting aboriginal people into that particular profession.
May 24, 1991

On May 16 I met with the representatives from the Dakota Ojibway Tribal Council regarding the funding concerns for policing services. The DOTCPD receives joint funding from both the federal government and the province of Manitoba. Despite the fact that operating costs continue to increase, neither of these governments will increase or commit to long-term funding before the national native policing review has been submitted. Although the initial report for the national native policing review was completed in January last year, an additional round of consultations pushed the date of this review that would be submitted to the cabinet back to January of this year. It would not be submitted to Treasury Board until the spring.
The DOTCPD handles about 95 per cent of the workload in eight reservations in Manitoba and has received requests for services from non-native communities, thus reducing the workload for the RCMP in these areas.
Without adequate support, this police department cannot perform its duties as effectively as possible. Native policing is an important and valuable program. It is beneficial for native communities to work with a police force which can speak and understand their own aboriginal language and which possesses a cultural understanding of the residents.
The history of the RCMP in the north has been a long and honourable one. The relationships that have been forged over the years are ones that are based on mutual respect and concern for the people who have lived there.
What has happened over the years is that as we have had recruitment, which is basically federally driven, we are being asked to pay for services to the tune of 75 per cent. Yet the policies all come from a federally driven process.
If we are going to have accountability and credibility of the work that is undertaken by the members of the forces and if the moneys are going to be paid by the territorial government, clearly there should be a greater input by the Minister of Justice in this case, who has responsibility for policing matters in the Northwest Territories. Clearly there has to be more of an input in terms of policy and the kind of mandate that they have and the kind of relationships that they build.

Even with regard to recruitment there has to be a greater effort to promote the idea of having suitable individuals come into remote communities. There is no orientation or familiarization process that meets and accommodates the needs of these people who are expected to go into communities where they have never been outside of looking at pictures and doing their own particular inquiries.
It is rather difficult at this time to look at the long history of the RCMP in the north and the relationships they have built and to forfeit that because we have additional financial pressures put on the territorial government. Yet they are distanced from the policy mandate that is given to that particular force to carry out.
The relationship in the past has been one that is based on mutual respect. The RCMP in the old days travelled by dog team. Their first commitment upon coming to a community was to meet with the leaders of that community, to make contacts, and to have an established communication strategy in terms of who they communicate with and just exactly what the people could expect. The expectations were varied. In many cases the RCMP provided services that were not within their mandate. They were expected to be there when someone died; they were expected to be there when someone was bom; they were expected to be there when there were emergencies; and to provide an extensive array of services.
These people cannot go unnoticed. I am proud to say that there is some progress. I am not one to sabotage the good work of the members who are there. What I would like to do is recognize that there are individuals who have come to the north and have contributed greatly. They have built very strong relationships with the people of the north and they should be recognized for that. In fact, it has been a great inspiration for many northerners to look at the whole profession of policing.
Just of late, we have sworn in a number of aboriginal people to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. These young people look forward to a career they feel will be challenging and will contribute to the betterment of life in the north.

May 24, 1991

The long-standing relationship with the aboriginal people is one based on a lot of creativity and ingenuity. We have, with the RCMP in the north, something worth preserving. Members of the RCMP have endured a lot of things that other members in other places do not necessarily realize until they come to the remote regions of our country. These include the fact that they are there for long periods of isolation. There are many expectations. They are sometimes on call 24 hours a day when they are alone. They are expected to provide a whole array of services.
There must be a way, within the recruitment process, to outline the variety of different services. There is a great deal of counselling, for instance, that goes on with regard to RCMP work.
The RCMP is much admired and it is a noble profession in my part of the world. It is a relationship that has grown through adversity at times, and a relationship that is well worth preserving and working for. There does not need to be the additional pressure of additional costs to serving in the north in a number of capacities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the motion of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi and I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak to it.
The federal government has been and remains strongly committed to the RCMP and to the contract policing program. We made a reasonable offer to the provinces and territories on September 29, 1989, to renew the contracts. We are more than willing to do just that.
The federal government believes that everyone is well served by having the RCMP provide provincial, territorial, and municipal policing services under contract. These arrangements give Canadians the highest possible professional standards on a national scale. Canadians in the contract provinces are getting some of the best and most economical policing services in the world.
The RCMP is one of the largest and most sophisticated law enforcement agencies in the world. It has grown from a small group of people who many years ago marched 800 miles across the prairies, often short of water and provisions, to establish authority throughout the west.
It is important that we understand some of the history surrounding this uniquely Canadian institution. The idea of a mounted police force originated in response to a need to establish law and order in the northwest in advance of settlement. The solution of Sir John A. Macdonald was the creation of a paramilitary police trained for plains warfare but with primarily civil responsibilities. Its model was the Royal Irish Constabulary.
Accordingly, in 1873 the Dominion Parliament passed legislation for the establishment of a mounted police
Supply
force for the Northwest Territories to be known as the North-West Mounted Police.
Three divisions of 50 men each were mobilized at Fort Garry, Manitoba where training and organization proceeded throughout the winter of 1873. Authority was subsequently granted to recruit up to the authorized strength of 300 members and another 150 men were recruited.
Once established in the northwest, demands on the force increased. Members supervised trading practices, provided some relief and medical services to Indians, and carried out patrols throughout the area.
In addition to having an economic effect, the arrival of the force and the collective social and cultural values of its members had an impact on the development of western Canada. On leaving the force, many members settled in the west and continued to have a permanent influence on their communities.
In 1883 the government increased the force's strength from 300 to 500 men in order to respond to growing responsibilities. Detachments and divisions were soon established in new urban centres and in railway settlements.
On account of the North-West Rebellion of 1885 the authorized strength of the force rose to 1,000. The Depot Division was created in November, 1885, to train recruits in Regina, which had become the headquarters of the force in 1882.
By the turn of the century new responsibilities had been assigned to the RCMP in the Canadian north. The gold rush in the Yukon became potentially troublesome as thousands upon thousands of prospectors came to the territory and converged on the tiny settlement of Dawson. The North-West Mounted Police was sent to impose order, and violence was kept to a minimum.
From the start, the mounted police carried out almost all the administrative functions of government. Its members acted as land agents, magistrates, police, mail carriers and so on. By 1899, after the peak of the rush had subsided, civil servants had relieved the force of many of its administrative duties.

Reports of abuse of natives and threats by European nations to Canadian sovereignty in the far north led to the opening of detachments in the eastern and western Arctic.
In 1904, in recognition of its many services to Canada, King Edward VII renamed the force The Royal NorthWest Mounted Police.
When the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were created in 1905 the first contracts were negotiated for the force to act under the direction of the provincial authorities to enforce criminal law and local statutes. The agreements required the dominion government to maintain and control 500 Royal North-West Mounted Police in the two provinces in return for annual payments of $75,000 each.
On all provincial matters of justice administration, the force was responsible, through the commissioner, to the provincial attorneys general. This arrangement gave the provinces a bargain as full police services to the new provinces had been costing two or three times as much as the amount set out in the agreement.
During the First World War the North-West Mounted Police was forced to withdraw policing services from Alberta and Saskatchewan, causing these provinces to organize their own police forces. After the armistice, however, the force absorbed the dominion police which had performed federal policing duties in eastern Canada and on February 1, 1920, became the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Madam Speaker, I have a well researched speech which outlines not only the history of the RCMP, but the contractual arrangements of the financing between the federal government, the provinces and municipalities. It is very much relevant to this debate. I am sorry if the member feels offended, but it is relevant and has a large bearing on the debate and I would like to continue, as I will.
For more than a decade after 1917 the RCMP policed only the Northwest and the Yukon Territories as well as being responsible for federal statutes. The matter of provincial policing was raised again in a letter dated November 20, 1926, from Saskatchewan Premier James Gardiner to federal Justice Minister Ernest Lapointe. It reads:
The policing of this force is rapidly developing into a condition which is likely to bring the whole matter into the field of political controversy. The main reason for this, to my mind, is that we are very much over-policed. We have a condition which developed during the war, which leaves us with virtually three police forces: the RCMP, the provincial police and the municipal police. The result is that there is overlapping, local friction, disagreement between different organizations, the appearance of too many uniformed men at every public gathering, (giving the appearance of a military occupation), and cost which, if continued, will develop into a first-class political issue.
That was the federal justice minister, Ernest Lapointe.
By 1932 the RCMP had assumed contracts to provide a provincial police force to Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island. The provincial contracts all expired at the end of May, 1935, and by May, 1937, all had been renewed to a variety of expiry dates. Though contracts for the provincial policing of British Columbia and Newfoundland were both signed in 1950, the idea was considered much earlier in British Columbia.
May 24, 1991

In 1932, when many other provinces moved to RCMP policing because of financial pressures, a committee studying policing in B.C. concluded that so large a territory with so sparse a population-700,000 people at that time-should economize by having one police force instead of 39 separate ones at the various levels of government. The federal commission arrived at the same recommendation in 1939.
At the beginning of 1950 the attorney general of British Columbia introduced legislation to empower his government to conduct negotiations with the federal government to contract the RCMP. He estimated annual provincial savings of $1.5 million by using the RCMP, taking into account the pressure for improved services and capital costs of necessary equipment and buildings.
In August, 1950, British Columbia and the federal government signed an agreement for the provision of provincial policing services by the RCMP. This contract also had the effect of doubling the municipal responsibilities of the RCMP. The British Columbia provincial police had formerly conducted municipal policing under 46 contracts throughout the province. All of these were taken on by the RCMP.
The RCMP began policing Newfoundland as a result of the entry of that province into Canada in 1949. Although the Newfoundland Rangers and the Newfoundland constabulary also represented long, local tradition, it was recognized that the RCMP would offer superior effectiveness with financial savings over a combination of federal and provincial forces. In August, 1950, a contract was signed with Newfoundland for the provision of RCMP provincial policing for $196,000 a year in contrast with the previous annual cost to Newfoundland of $550,000 for the rangers and for the constabulary. The province arranged for the construction and location of new prefabricated housing and detachment buildings. The Royal Newfoundland Constabulary was to continue policing St. John's. Seventy-three rangers and 37 constabulary members joined the RCMP.
The RCMP became involved in municipal policing because municipalities in the depression years began applying for their services under contract. In January,

1932, the mayor of Calgary directed his city council to consider the merits of the RCMP policing that city. The suggestion did not go anywhere at that time. In any case, the RCMP Act of that time appeared to prohibit the enforcement of municipal by-laws.
Persistent requests culminated in an initial experiment in 1935 of a three-man municipal detachment at Flin Flon, Manitoba. In 1936 the RCMP Act was amended empowering the Governor General in Council to authorize the RCMP to enter into municipal contracts. The Flin Flon arrangement was confirmed retroactively in 1936.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The only town besides Flin Flon to receive RCMP policing by contract during this time was Melville, Saskatchewan. By the end of the decade it became clear that the two municipal contracts were appealing examples to an increasing number of applicants and procedures were generalized. In 1940 the commissioner of the RCMP was authorized to conclude municipal agreements on behalf of the federal government.
The third municipality to receive RCMP policing was Humboldt, Saskatchewan, and it was quickly followed by a succession of others. At first most of the communities were in Manitoba and Saskatchewan but the maritimes and Alberta soon had municipal contracts as well.
By March, 1946, 68 towns and cities in the contract provinces were being policed by the RCMP. Six were in the maritimes and the other 62 were in the prairies. By 1951 the addition of the British Columbia municipalities brought the number of RCMP municipal contracts to 119. Today the number stands at 191.

May 24, 1991
Supply
From early on the federal government recognized the limited federal benefit of municipal policing and in 1941 the commissioner of the day declared that the force was only interested in municipal policing where some locational or other advantage to the federal policing role could be achieved. Initially the cost sharing for municipal contracts was the same as that of the provincial contracts. Costs were rising and the force realized that municipal RCMP officers were devoting their full time to the towns while those doing provincial contract work usually carried out federal duties as well. The possibility of requiring municipalities to pay more than was demanded from the provinces was debated in the late 1940s.
As the latest contracts expired on March 31 of this year, provinces were paying 70 per cent and the federal government paid 30 per cent of the costs of municipal policing. The cost share with municipalities with a population under 15,000 people was 70 per cent municipal and 30 per cent federal. For municipalities with populations over 15,000, the split was 90 per cent municipal and 10 per cent federal.
The federal offer of renewal that is currently on the table proposes that within the next 10 years the provinces pay 75 per cent of the costs of policing their province. The offer proposes the costs to municipalities with a population of less than 5,000 increase from 70 per cent to 75 per cent. The cost to municipalities with a population between 5,000 and 15,000 increases from 70 per cent to 85 per cent.
Finally, the costs of policing services to municipalities with populations in excess of 15,000 increase from 90 per cent to 95 per cent.
An important fact to remember is that even at 100 per cent of the costs, the RCMP continues to present an economical and efficient police service. The RCMP has a clear cost advantage over independent police services.
In conclusion, the history of the RCMP is an integral part of the history of this country. I repeat what I said at the opening of my remarks: The federal government is strongly committed to the RCMP and to contract policing. We have made an offer and we look forward to the provinces coming to the table to negotiate an agreement
acceptable to all parties in order that these contracts can be renewed.

With great respect for the parliamentary secretary, they have to try to find some warm-blooded westerner who will get up and defend the government on the RCMP. Again, I am just surmising because I used to be a parliamentary secretary, but this poor gentleman across from us had to go and find a warm, live, breathing member from western Canada who would read the kind of drivel we just heard. What did he tell us, buried among the pearls in his speech? Did he tell us that we were overpoliced in Canada? Was that the point he was trying to make? He can ask another question afterward if I misunderstood him.
Let me try to get to the issues that are at stake here. I confess that for over 12 years I worked with the members of the RCMP in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, and here in Ottawa to a degree, so I have une faiblesse pour la Gendarmerie royale du Canada. I have also worked with municipal police and city police.
One of the things that they do not understand on the other side of the House is that a village policeman in a small municipality in Manitoba has difficulty giving a ticket to the son or daughter of the mayor of the village. This is one of the reasons why western Canadians, all 7.5 million of us, and Atlantic Canadians I am sure, like members of the RCMP. It is because carry out their job without fear or favour. They do not care if they are giving a ticket to-at least this is what I believe-the mayor's daughter, the Speaker's daughter or son, or even the Prime Minister's daughter or son, no offence to the sons and daughters. That is why the RCMP has been respected in western Canada, in northern Canada, and in Atlantic Canada.
I hope the hon. parliamentary secretary will tell us, if he gets up after this talk, about this canard that westerners, northerners, and Atlantic Canadians are subsidizing the people in Ontario and Quebec. Who does the parliamentary secretary think pays for the members who are outside guarding this building? Who does he think is paying for, I gather, 2,000 members of the RCMP in Ontario and Quebec if it is not taxpayers in Atlantic Canada, northern Canada, and western Canada? Do not tell me, please, that the provincial budgets of Ontario or Quebec are paying for that, because they are not. I understand all Canadians are paying for the 2,000 men and women in the RCMP in Quebec and about the same number in Ontario.
I understand that back in 1981 it was agreed that the provinces would pay 70 per cent because about 70 per cent of the police work was Criminal Code and provincial statutes. As you know, the enforcement of the law of the Criminal Code across Canada is a provincial responsibility. The provinces agreed to pay 70 per cent. The federal government agreed to pay 30 per cent because about 30 per cent of RCMP work is federal statutes such as the Narcotic Control Act. In municipalities the formula was 90 per cent-10 per cent. The ratio was different in municipalities like Edmonton where the member who just spoke is from and therefore there was a 90 per cent-10 per cent formula.
The other reason they agreed on the 70-30 split was the efficiency argument. It was far better to have one police force, where it was acceptable, than to have two. The third reason they agreed on the 70-30 formula was because of national unity. The RCMP is a symbol of our country and is very important. When has it been more important to have a symbol of national unity, such as the RCMP, than right now?
The same government which gave a throne speech last week telling us that it is trying to do something about national unity will try this week, or the next time it gets contracts with the provinces, as the member for York South-Weston mentioned, to increase the burden on municipalities.

If I may say a word about Alberta. In my province 61 out of 291 municipalities contract services from the RCMP, and 44 per cent of Albertans, or about 1.1 million people, live under the jurisdiction of the RCMP detachments. The current cost-share ratio for contracted RCMP services was established in 1981. Both the municipalities and the federal government believed a 30 per cent federal share of RCMP cost was an adequate contribution.
The government is in effect saying to the municipalities across the country, outside of Ontario and Quebec, that they can either maintain existing RCMP services by cutting costs elsewhere or they can cut RCMP services at the risk of endangering public safety and emergency

responsiveness. What the member for Western Arctic said about the north and the traditional role of the RCMP applies just as much in western Canada and, I am sure, in Atlantic Canada. The person people call on when they have virtually any kind of problem, including the birth of a child, is the RCMP officer who is there in two minutes. I do not know how many babies the RCMP has delivered, but I am sure it is a lot.
If the contracts are going to force municipalities and provinces to pay 16 per cent more for the RCMP in unincorporated areas, that will cause the public safety to suffer in those areas.
The Nielsen task force and the federal law enforcement review talk a lot about these issues. I do not believe anybody on the other side has mentioned them today but I have not been here for all the speeches.
Gary Browning, on behalf of the Alberta Urban Municipalities Association, has not received any satisfactory response to the association's inquiries.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities has requested a meeting on this matter on behalf of its members from the eight contracting provinces, and it has yet to receive a response.
What kind of government would turn down-it may have given up on Alberta-the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, which represents three-quarters of the 26 million or 27 million of us in this country? What kind of government would turn down a meeting with that federation on a matter of such fundamental importance as this?

It could possibly go into a crisis situation and be somehow beyond any kind of bias or compromise. It could be beyond the realm of the immediate crisis and not have any serious problems or doubts about its credibility in that jurisdiction. I could point to the logging issue in B.C. I could look at Lubicon, which was referred to, and at James Bay. A number of places need a force that is above compromise and is unbiased as such. On the question of the member, he might be interested that Colonel James Macleod went from Winnipeg to Alberta. He was a commissioner of the North-West Mounted Police. When he died as a judge in Alberta, or the Northwest Territories as it was then, there was not a single dime of a pension for his wife Mary. I think they had three or four children and she found it extremely difficult to get by in the years after that. Some ranchers from southern Alberta basically pitched in and helped her out.

May 24, 1991
Supply
Why do I cite that? It shows that things have not always been easy for the RCMP and that even some of the giants like Colonel Macleod, at least his wife and children afterwards, did not find it easy in the days before they had pensions for anybody in the RCMP.
It is a deeply ingrained part of our history. We take pride whether it is in southern Manitoba or northern Alberta or the western Arctic. The RCMP is a symbol of Canada and these morons on the opposite side are doing everything they can to try to make it more difficult to maintain that symbol. These days, symbols are extremely important to this country.
