subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, despite the pain that the government's proposal in the RCMP contract negotiations is giving to a number of Canadians, I still welcome the opportunity to be able to make a few comments on behalf of not only my own constituents but a number of my colleagues and their constituencies from around the country, particularly in the province of British Columbia.
I should begin by briefly reading the motion that my New Democratic Party colleague from Comox-Albemi presented to the House today. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take into full account the budgetary reality of the provinces and municipalities involved in Royal Canadian Mounted Police contract negotiations and therefore be prepared to negotiate a contract for RCMP services which does not unfairly transfer policing costs from the federal government to provincial and municipal governments.
One of the members opposite noted earlier that we had phrased this motion in as civilized a way as possible in order to encourage the government to think again that when it is transferring burdens, as it seems to want to do time and time again, it seems to have a proclivity to transfer them to those Canadian taxpayers and those assemblies of Canadian taxpayers least able to pay. In this case, that is the smaller municipalities, the small villages and cities that spread right across this country, particularly Atlantic Canada, the west and the province of British Columbia.
The eight provinces unanimously rejected the federal proposition to raise the provincial share of Mountie policing costs by an additional $79 million. We have a lot of company in our protest.
Policing contracts between the RCMP and eight provinces expired at the beginning of April. The ten-year deal covers all provinces, except Quebec and Ontario, which have their own provincial police forces.
May 24, 1991

Under the proposed agreement the Mounties provide provincial policing and some municipal services in the eight provinces at a total annual cost of $761 million. The provinces pay 70 per cent and the federal government pays 30 per cent.
What Ottawa wants to do with the current proposal is change that formula to 75 per cent paid by the provinces and municipalities and 25 per cent by the federal government. That would cost an additional $79 million to those jurisdictions least able to pay.
At this point I would like to pay some tribute to a number of my colleagues who have fought very hard over the period of the last number of weeks to raise this issue with the government in as non-confrontational a way as possible, hoping that they would be able to appeal to the conscience of those on the other side of the House to recognize the severe difficulties which people in small town western Canada, in particular, are having.
The member for Okanagan-Shuswap, in particular, arranged a meeting two weeks ago, on May 8, in the city of Vernon, with all of my British Columbia New Democratic Party colleagues and a representative of the Union of B.C. Municipalities.
She did a tremendous job of outlining for us very clearly the issues that were at stake for them and the financial implications of this almost dogmatic pursuit of their unreasonable proposal by the federal government.
Others who have taken a major part in our campaign to get the government to change its mind have been the members for Kamloops, Okanagan-Similkameen- Merritt, Kootenay East and Prince George-Bulkley Valley, as well as our party's federal critic, the member for Brant.
We have not met with any more success at this point than have the eight representatives of those provincial governments that are being seriously impacted by the government's very hard-nosed bargaining stance on this issue. One can hardly call it bargaining because while the federal government and the Solicitor General have been prepared to discuss estimates of the cost base, when it comes to cost share they said simply: "That is not negotiable; you have our position; take it or leave it; we will cancel the agreements."
Supply
At one point they were threatening that the police contracts would simply end at the beginning of April. Thankfully we have gone beyond that point and they have withdrawn to a more reasonable position. I would still hope that we can come up with some kind of interim agreement or at least a phasing-in proposal by the federal government. This has been suggested by a number of municipalities in order to provide some breathing space at least and as an indication of good faith to those municipalities and provincial governments, especially those smaller municipalities that need time if they are going to adjust to the kind of financial impacts the government's proposal will place on them if it does go ahead as it is proposing.
The proposal by the federal government of new contracts calls for municipalities to pay an extra 5 per cent to 27 per cent for policing costs. That is the impact. We say that move is an unfair burden on local ratepayers and particularly hard on very small communities. The cut amounts to an extra unfair tax for Canadians who choose to live in smaller towns.
Canadians in rural communities are already hurting from post office cuts, CBC cuts, and the downsizing of VIA Rail. They have the same right to police protection as do citizens in larger metropolitan areas.
We call on the government to negotiate a new contract which does not unfairly transfer policing costs from the federal level to provincial and municipal governments.
I would just like to mention a couple of examples. In my own constituency, the city of Castlegar will have to come up with about $25,000 more this year for policing services if Ottawa's proposal to decrease its share of RCMP costs goes through. The city paid $508,000 last year for 10 officers. Under the government's proposal, the city would pay $533,000 for nine officers. More money for less service.
The B.C. solicitor general, Mr. Ivan Mesmer, who has been negotiating this agreement with the federal government, has said quite clearly that these municipalities do not think it is fair. He explained that in communities such as Williams Lake, 40 per cent of the municipal budget will go toward policing if the municipality's share of policing costs is increased, as it will be if the federal government's proposal becomes fact.

May 24, 1991
Supply
This is veiy serious. In a letter which I received in late March from the city of Trail in my own constituency, the mayor, Sandor Santori, points out that the city's share of policing in the city of Trail in 1990 amounted to $705,000 from a total cost of $1,007,904. A 3 per cent increase to that cost base will bring the city's share to $726,699 from a total of $1,038,141.
With the proposal from the federal government to increase the cost base from 70 per cent to 85 per cent, the city's share of policing costs will increase by $176,888. This would represent a 5.25 per cent increase over the city's 1990 total taxation of $3.37 million to $3,543 million.
To the individual taxpayer, this represents an increase of $20 per residential property. In the case of the city's largest taxpayer, Cominco, it is an increase of $120,000.
I need hardly point out to cabinet ministers who come from western Canada, especially those who are somewhat familiar with the history of Cominco, that this is the time when it can ill afford any other large tax expenditure.
It has been hit very hard by astronomical increases in water charges from the province of British Columbia in the last few years, which have been totally unjustified. The federal government is a shareholder in Cominco's current modernization program. It should be aware as a shareholder that there are severe financial restrictions on that company at the moment.
Many people in the community of Trail and surrounding areas feel very threatened by a somewhat shaky future as a result of the difficulties they are having in adapting to the new technologies.
The past Solicitor General said in the House of Commons that there is one reality that has to be taken into consideration and that is the cost of the RCMP borne by the federal government.
He also stated in a press release that his offer of a 5 per cent increase was "designed to redistribute the net costs more fairly so that those who use the services assume an appropriate measure of the cost".
This is proof that in setting up his strategy, his office has completely disregarded the fiscal reality in which municipalities have been placed, thanks to a multitude of policies set up by his own government over the last six years.
This time, thanks to the structure of these agreements, the government has managed to download its responsibility on to the third level of government, especially small- and medium-sized municipalities.
We feel that this is one more indication-if we needed one-that this government and the Conservative Party are just totally out of touch. In its blind rush to deal with only the federal deficit, it has managed to undermine the very fabric of this country with cuts to VIA Rail, the CBC, the Forest Resource Development Agreement, postal services, and the sale of Petro-Canada.
This is now threatening the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and its presence at the community level in much of this country. At a time when Canada's future is on the line, this government cannot afford to play high roller with one of this country's most respected institutions.
It worries me when I ask myself the question: What is this government's bottom line? What is our bottom line? Our bottom line is Canada, and I hope it is theirs, too. I am sure, in their hearts, it is.
Judging by what the government does, more and more Canadians are having a difficult time believing that.
A few months ago, I had an opportunity to spend some time with a gentleman from the Golden Horseshoe in central Canada who was a major manufacturer of pollution control equipment. He is a major real estate developer. He has agricultural estates in Central America and he moves in a circle in which I do not normally move.
He is not a person who puts much credence in conspiracy theories or anything like it, but in trying to determine what the economic policy of the government and the rationale for it was, he said that he and his associates were saying that they could not understand what the reason for the government's approach was to the Canadian economy, unless it was to attempt to force Canadians into becoming Americans.
May 24, 1991

That is the only one that seemed to make any sense if you followed all the courses of action that this government is following. I do not believe that, and they do not believe it. Nobody wants to believe it.
You see the artificially high price of the Canadian dollar. There is the emasculation of one Canadian institution after another and you hear the Prime Minister coming up with words to the effect that Canada is more than a few Crown corporations and a few national programs.
Yet we begin to ask if we continue to destroy all those national programs, all those national institutions and all those national services, how long it will be before some Canadians begin to say: "If we have this huge bureaucracy and this expensive government and all we have got left is an anthem and a flag, maybe we ought to wonder what the hell we are doing as Canadians"?
That is what they are going to ask if we start removing all of the symbols and all of the services that we have so carefully and thoughtfully built up over decades and decades since those first Canadians, as an article of faith, said to themselves: "Even though this nation called Canada is not an economic unit, by a political act of will we want it to be a separate, identifiable nation and community".
This country was not created because it made a lot of economic sense. A small ribbon of population stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and to the Arctic is not a natural economic unit. This country was built because people wanted something different and something distinctive and the government is wrecking it. I do not believe it is consciously doing it. However, if it wants to leave these decisions up to the glories of the marketplace in some kind of doctrinaire, dogmatic belief that what is good for General Motors is good for the country, what is good for whomever it happens to be-Richardson in Winnipeg or the Bronfmans or whomever-then we are . in serious trouble in this country and we are not going to have a country left.
I just want to return briefly to the presentation that the Union of B.C. Municipalities made to us on May 8 in Vernon, B.C. The UBCM did an excellent job. I am sure many members of the government have read its submission, and I would ask them to look at it carefully again.
Supply
On the first page of that submission, the UBCM points out very clearly why those of us from British Columbia are perhaps more worked up and more concerned about the impact of this particular proposal than almost anyone else across the country. In fact, all three speakers from my party today in this debate have been from the province of British Columbia.
People from British Columbia, a province with only 10 per cent of the population, comprise 27 per cent of the RCMP force in Canada, 39 per cent of the RCMP contract force in Canada, and 63 per cent of the RCMP municipal contract force in Canada.
If members were wondering why we are acting and behaving as though this particular action of the federal government singles out British Columbia and its taxpayers and small and medium-sized communities for punishment, the reason is because 63 per cent of the RCMP municipal contract force in Canada comes from our province. I think we have a reason to be a little annoyed.
There are three issues to be resolved: the cost base, the cost shares, and accountability. The position of the UBCM, which is one that we share, is that on the cost base issue there is no disagreement that there are items which can be negotiated where there is a good business reason, for example UIC payments for federal civilian staff. With respect to cost shares, however, we remain firm in our view that there should be no increases.
Finally, there also must be improved accountability so that we are assured that we are getting the best value for the dollar spent.
Why should members on the government side support the position of B.C. municipalities on the cost issue?
First, the federal benefit has not diminished since the last contract. Second, federal costs would increase if the federal government did not enjoy the economies of scale of municipal policing. Third, federal costs to maintain a national force for internal and external emergencies would increase. Fourth, the contribution to national unity is beyond dollars and cents. We do not put a price on Canada.
Finally, what the UBCM and British Columbians from one end of the province to the other are asking for is initially an interim agreement.

May 24, 1991
Supply
B.C. has been without a policing contract since April 1. This situation cannot continue. We urge the government to immediately enter into an interim agreement with a retroactive provision as proposed by the province of British Columbia.
We support a new federal negotiating direction. We urge the government to support a resumption of negotiations in which federal negotiators have more latitude to negotiate cost-base issues, to approach phasing in a total cost framework, and to quantify the federal benefits that are reflected in the current cost shares.
In the 1984 election the Prime Minister defined Canada as a nation of small towns with big dreams. We hope that it is the intention of this government, as I am sure it is, and as it is of all of us, that small town Canadians should have more than dreams. They should have the right to the same standard of services as other Canadians whose circumstances have put in larger metropolitan areas and in the heartland of this continent.
We produce much of the wealth of this nation in small town Canada. As a result of that we often undergo much greater variations in our economies and much higher levels of unemployment more often than central Canada, even though central Canada is undergoing some tough times right now. We undergo really serious times every four or five years when 1,500 people are out of work in a town of only 6,000 people, sometimes permanently. We are used to that sort of thing. We in small town Canada in the west, in the east, and particularly in the province of British Columbia-because it is so seriously impacted by this government proposal-have a right to equality of treatment. We demand it. We ask the government to think again, to be more flexible in its approach and give us a deal that we can live with.

There are a number of us, perhaps myself included, who wish that people with important agendas would sometimes not tamper with things that really do not have to be tampered with, that unduly upset people, perhaps for no positive reason that can be seen.
Again, there is a strong perception in many parts of Canada that we are changing, that our international relationships have changed, that our broader loyalties, at least outside of Canada, have been changing. Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the comments of the hon. member. I have a couple of questions and a couple of comments.
With the cabinet shuffle and the new Solicitor General, certainly it is my hope that negotiations between the provinces and the RCMP for RCMP services will take a much more constructive and realistic tack. I think it is very important that the contract be signed. That contract, though, has to be fair and reasonable. I feel that the cost-sharing agreement of 70-30 should remain as it is.
In my province of Prince Edward Island, municipalities are financially strapped. They really have not got any more money to pay for RCMP services. What we have here is simply another example of government members passing on their budgetary problems to other levels of government. They have already shirked their financial obligations in the area of health. They have discarded their responsibilities in the area of education, diminished their commitments in the area of social services, and now they are looking to partially abandon their commitment to policing, safety and security.
May 24, 1991

I have a couple of questions that I would like to ask the hon. member. I wonder if he would agree that the direction the government is taking to date is a further shirking of its responsibilities to communities across the country who require the service.
Would the member not admit that the diminishing of the federal government's commitment to funding RCMP services is another example of this government passing its financial problems on to other levels of government?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 -ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been in the House all day and I have had a chance to listen to the debate. I have a couple of comments before I start to address the topic specifically.
I find it rather lamentable that when we get into this kind of a debate about a very important issue, not only because of what the RCMP does but because of the esteem in which the RCMP is held across the country, we have not had a chance to have more genuine discussion of the actual issue itself.
I am not so sure that it adds anything to the demeanour of the House to have the member for Edmonton Southeast get up and complain about the way a member was delivering his speech. Some of us deliver speeches in various ways. Some of us take a lot of time and put a lot of thought into preparing speeches and doing homework and, as a result, like to refer more than others to a prepared text. I think that is something that should be left to the individual. I know what the House rules are, but I am not so sure that to get up and simply complain
Supply
about the way somebody is delivering a speech adds much to the tone and to the substance of the debate. I also do not think it does anything useful to call people names, which we witnessed this afternoon. We were called morons. I don't think that is very becoming as far as intelligent debate and discussion in this House.
We are talking about something that is very important. The RCMP, the policing of our country, and the way we govern the conduct between ourselves, is very fundamental to any country. I think it would help in terms of the way we think of ourselves and look at ourselves as a country if we could have more of the respect between people on either side of the aisle that we all hold for the RCMP. I find it unfortunate that we did not get a chance to discuss more of the issue.
I would like in the few minutes that are remaining to talk about the issue in some perspective. We are not, and there has never been any suggestion of, withdrawing services. This has been suggested by members and I do not know where it comes from. There has never been any suggestion by any member of the government that if there could not be a satisfactory conclusion to negotiation by a certain period of time there were going to be services withdrawn. That is simply not so. That is unacceptable I think to all sides of the House, unacceptable to Canadians generally, and something that this government has never ever talked about getting into.
Second, it has been suggested that what the Solicitor General is proposing is going to gut the RCMP by implication. Gut is a pretty strong word and it conjures up some pretty fatal images, if you will. We are not talking about that at all.
Let me give you some numbers, Madam Speaker, to back that up. If you use 1988-89 as the fiscal year just for comparison, the total cost of running the RCMP across the country was approximately $1.2 billion, a lot of money. Of that amount, approximately $500 million, and these are round numbers, was used for policing that was directly attributable to responsibilities that are solely that of the federal government. That leaves approximately $700 million that is work that is done on a cost shared arrangement with the provinces and with the municipalities. That number has not been used.

May 24, 1991
Supply
Let us talk about the $700 million which, and again these are round numbers, the provinces are being charged now at the rate of about 7 per cent, which in round numbers again is about $500 million. Let me talk a little bit about how that cost sharing is done.
There is no charge in that cost share for any of the capital improvements. Any of the barracks that are constructed, any of the buildings that are built, which amounts to approximately $35 million, are not charged to the provinces or the municipalities. That kind of funding is totally a federal expense.
In addition to that, when we sit down to work out a rental fee, a rental charge if you will for the use of those barracks, the rental charge that has been used has been $5 a square foot of which the provinces presently pay 70 per cent. That means that that is $3.50 a square foot that the provinces are being asked to pay.
If we compare what the provinces charge us when they rent us similar facilities in municipal situations for which the RCMP use, the provinces charge us $15 a square foot.
Let us talk about the over-all issue in terms of that kind of number. We again are not talking about withdrawing services. We are not talking about anything that is in any way going to destroy the RCMP. We are talking about what seems to me is something reasonable in terms of moving some of the costs from the federal government where we think it should be more appropriately and that is in the area of the provinces and the municipalities.
Additionally, there are many things that the federal government does with the RCMP that are totally a federal responsibility. That is not something that we are asking the provinces to cost share.
In many ways it is unfair to the RCMP, to the force itself, to have some of these suggestions that I have heard today put out. That is not in fact what the government is proposing to do.
I want to say a little bit about transfer payments. The hon. member from Strathcona who called us names and then left the House was asking if we were going to explain how Manitoba was going to find an additional $90 million over the next 10 years. I have checked with
people in the Department of Solicitor General and they have no idea where this number came from. As far as I can see, it is a fictitious number.
First of all, we are not talking about a one-shot deal if we can conclude a successful negotiation, and I say if. Whatever cost increases there are, whatever is done, it is going to be phased in, likely over a considerable number of years, maybe five years, maybe even ten years. To suggest again that the province of Manitoba is going to be asked to find an additional $90 million over 10 years has no foundation in any of the numbers that I have been able to check out. I do not think it is possible, because negotiations are under way, to give a precise number, but if you are asking me what the number would be, my guess is it would be, at most, less than half of what the member was talking about.
The member from Prince Edward Island talked about reducing transfer payments. I want to give her some numbers. In 1984-85 when we came to government, the province of Prince Edward Island received from the federal government in transfer payments, $207.1 million. In 1990-91, the fiscal year just concluded, it received $313.9 million, an increase of over 50 per cent. It needs to be put in that kind of a context because to listen to the opposition today, you would think that all the federal government had been doing was reducing our responsibilities. That belies the numbers. As I stated earlier, there was a 50 per cent increase for the province of Prince Edward Island.
In my own province of Manitoba, the number has gone from approximately $1.2 billion of transfers to the province from the federal government in 1984-85, to about $1.9 billion in 1990-91, which is an increase of $700 million. Again, these are transfers of additional money to help the provinces meet their responsibilities in various areas of health care, social assistance, and those kinds of programs.
I see the member from Kootenay West is here. Let us talk a little bit about his province of British Columbia. When we came to government in 1984, the province of British Columbia received from the federal government about $2.26 billion. The previous fiscal year, the one just concluded, the province received a little over $3.1 billion, again a substantial increase of about $800 million since we have been the government.

With some of the increased costs that we are asking the provinces to pay, we have also been transferring to the provinces additional money to meet some of those responsibilities.
If you look at some of the benefits we have from having a national police force, the estimates that I have seen-and they have been done basically by an arm of Statistics Canada-indicate that the policing costs we charge to the provinces for the services rendered by the RCMP and the kind of quality of service they get, the continuity right across the country, the ability to enforce different acts federally and provincially, if each little municipality or each province was going to do it separately it would probably cost something like two and a half times as much as it does by having the national police force.
The member for Kootenay West who just spoke talked about economies of scale. He is absolutely right, but it works both ways. It is better for us to work together, which we are suggesting we do in this cost-sharing arrangement, again bearing in mind that we are not asking the provinces to cost-share the full amount of operating the RCMP, just the portion that is attributable to some of these joint arrangements between provinces and the municipalities. We are much better off to do this together, because there is a cost saving. It varies, I am told, from about two times as much in the west to as much as three times or three and a half times as much in the maritimes. And in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories it is even larger because of the sparse population. The member spoke on that, and she is absolutely right.
If we could have had that kind of a discussion, it seems to me it would have been of a lot more service to the force, which we all respect. Again I want to say we are not trying to gut the force. What we are simply trying to do is arrive at some fiscal arrangements that make more
Supply
sense. After all, the provinces are sovereign within their own borders and when it comes to fiscal and taxation matters, they have full responsibility. I sometimes wonder, as a premier of a province and a leader of the province, what some of their responsibilities are, other than to complain about the federal government not doing enough for them.
Having said that, and just to conclude, and to set the member's mind at ease I hope, and I hope he would take me at face value, we are not talking about doing anything except what he suggested, and that is, phasing in over a period of time, adjustments if we can agree on them as to how these costs are going to be increased.
If we could have had some of that discussion today I think we could have done a better job of presenting the issue, having a rational discussion on where this federal government is going to find money to do all the things we are asked to do, to keep the deficit under control, to keep interest rates coming down, which they have been doing for the last period of time, and I think they are probably four or five percentage points less than they have been. That is all part of our fiscal management. If interest rates go up, the opposition screams at us because we are not doing things to get interest rates down. When we do what seems to me to be reasonable things, to ask people to share in a little more of the cost of doing some things that we all want to keep, then we are chastised for it.
